WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Highland Season.—The Scottish season will he j marked this year by an unusually large number of ' Royal visits, one of the most interesting being the visit of the King and Queen of Spain to Lord and Lady Leith at Fyvie Castle in Aberdeenshire. Queen Alexandra and Princess Victoria will also spend a longer time on Deeside than on former occasions, and the King will be in residence at Balmoral later on in the season. The Prince and Princess of Wales with their children will be at Abergeldie, while the Princess Royal and the , Duke of Fife who always spend at least four months of the year in Scotland with their daughters, divide ; their time between Duff House, Bauffshire, and Mar I Lodge, Aberdeenshire, Princess Christian, and Princess Victoria of Schleswig l, Holstein, are ao to pay a visit to Sir Reginald and Lady Gordon Cathcart at Cluny Castle, in the same country, during September. • A Famous Picture.—The picture by Reynolds of "Lady Cockburn and her Children " which the late M. Alfred Beet has left to the National Gallery,origin- ally belonged to one of the most ancient families in Scotland. The lady in the picture was the daughter of Dr. Ayscougb? Dean of Bristol, who was married to Sir James Cockburn, the sixth baronet, and M.P. for Peeblesshire in 1762. The baronetey dated from 1627, but became extinct with the death of Lord Chief Justice Cockburn in 1880, and afterwards the Reynolds picture was exhibited for some years in the National Gallery, it having passed as a gift to the nation. There I was however, some flaw in the title to thus dispose of I it, and the picture had to be sold. It was bought by I by M. Beet for £22,000, and this famous picture for which Sir Joshua Reynolds received 175 guineas will once more take its place as one of the gems of the National Gallery. The Yachting Carnival.—The presence of the King and Queen of Spain has added greatly to the gaiety of the yachting season at Cowes, for hich spirits and youthful mirth are infectious, and such inspirations are always in evidence wherever their Majesties go. To them the visit to the Isle of Wight is more of a holiday jaunt, for the Queen of Spain, like our Prince of Wales, has never been a very enthusiastic yachtswoman, although she has often made short cruises with her mother, Princess Henry of Battenberg, on board the steam yacht Sheila. Our own Queen takes a keen interest in the contests of the racing craft, and there are of course many lovers of the sea amongst well- known women in Society. Lady Ormonde and her daughter, Lady Constance Butler, both take a practical interest in yachting, and are frequently out on the racers at Cowes. The 'Marchioness of Londonderry and the Countess of Dudley are also devoted to the sport, and have gained much of their experience in the handling of small yachts and sailing boats on the Irish loughs. Among other enthusiastic sailors are Lady Albemarle, the Duchess of St. Alban's, Lady Annesley, Lady Iveagh, Mrs. George Cornwallis West, and Mrs. Deck-Cnnyngham. A Fine Summer.—The fashionable gatherings of the past season have all been favoured with exceptionally fine weather. The brilliant sunshine ahich made Ascot and Henley such notable successes,vvas no less a feature at Goodwood, where summer toilettes were seen at their best, and added a wonderful charm to the natural beauty of the surniondings. Whatever the holiday season may have in store for as, we cannot cemplain that the weather has not afforded us every opportunity for don- ning our best and smartest summer frocks. When the year opened, the weather prophets told us that we were in for a cycle of wet and miserable seasons, and they pointed to the volcanic eruptions and earthquakes as tending to support these gloomy anticipations. They have not only been pleasantly falsified, but so far our summer has beaten all records in the matter of sunshine. I

Dress at Cowes.—The fabrics in evidence at Cowes are extremely various, and some of them must strike the observant as being very curious. Scouring cloth for example is the material chosen for many a smart yachting gown, and tea-cloth cotton is employed for dressy shore toilettes, while Oxford shirting of a coarse make is being used for shirts. By the uninitiated it iroay well be imagined that some Society women at least have turned over a new leaf, and are eschewing expen- sive costumes, but as a matter of fact the gown of scouring cloth is little if any cheaper than the linen or serge costume. The cost of making is the same, and the trimmings are usually of a more elaborate nature than when a better fabric is employed. Seaside and Travelling Hats.—Panamas are less seen than they have been during the past two or three summers, their place in our affections having been usurped by the neat French sailor, which is certainly much smarter, and generally more becoming than the ' floppy panama. For travelling the small round mush- room, raised at the side or back to suit the wearer, and simply trimmed with choux of ribbon, and a couple of quills, or white wings, is in the best of taste, but j whereas the French sailor can be made to suit almost ' every face, the mushroom is by no means so easy of manipulation. For yachting, many women are causing the black peak to be added to their cloth, serge, pique, or silk caps, and without doubt the addition is an immense improvement. The Length of Skirts.—One hardly knows whether the Rational Dress League is still in existence, so little do we hear about it nowadays, but, if it is, it will welcome the German example of issuing draconian orders, with regard to women's dress. In some of the German towns, the municipal authorities have decreed that women must not wear skirts which trail the ground, at any rate in the public streets. The order has been issued for sanitary reasons, but its peremptory character has aroused opposition, and a league of resist- ance has been formed. It is pointed out that while the authorities may be within their right to pro- hibit skirts being trailed, they cannot interfere with the length of women's dresses, provided they are not allowed to sweep the public streets, or roadways. Most women have reasons of their own for not wishing to soil their frocks in this way, but there is a likelihood of busy times in store for the police, if they are to interfere every time they see a skirt dropped, or touch- ing the ground. The Safest Trees in a Storm.—The fact that two men were killed by lightning, whilst sheltering beneath a beech tree, near Barnsley, last week, has caused con- siderable discussion and comment. The beach has, from time immemorial, been regarded as the safest of all trees in a thunderstorm, it being the rarest event for one to be struck. According to an eminent cateoro- logist. the oak is the most dangerous tree in a storm, tall pines coming next, while the beech affords the safest shelter. After rain, he goes on to say, trees are not so apt to split asunder with the stroke, as before it.
MADGE.

COMMERCIAL FAlLURES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of Commercial Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, August 3rd, was 163, viz. :—New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 91; Deeds of Arrangement registered,72. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 97 ; Deeds of Arrangement 38—total 185; being a decrease of 22. The total num- ber of Commercial Failures recorded during the 31 weeks of the present year is 5,102; the total number recorded in the corresponding 31 weeks of last year was 5,119, showing a decrease of 317.

African traveller has ever done an important journey without being reported dead a score of times. She was comforted a little. And then the Paris papers said it was a Frenchman, and at Berlin it was said to be a German. And after that a scandal swallowed columns of news, and there was no room for mere speculations about a stray English captain carrying the flag in a wilderness. But Madge read all the papers eagerly, and never opened one without a shiver. She and her mother hardly spoke. The momentary feeling of sorrow in the elder woman passed away when she found Madge bitter .and inexorable. She relapsed into sullen obstinacy, and was really ill for once. But even in sickness she maintained the hardest air of having been ill-used. She posed as a martyr to the nurse and recovered as if it were a spiteful duty. She talked to a select company of county dowagers concerning an ungrateful daughter, and a husband who did not know his duty to his class or his own name. She thanked Heaven for the death of Blundell and grew more devout. A letter from Billy comforted Madge more than anything else. He knew now, for his father sent him the news that his sister was engaged, and when he wrote he congratulated her with absolute delight. His mother sent a counterblast, and the answer was undiplomatic to a degree. He sang psalms about Richard Blundell, and said \that Madge was a lucky girl to get such a 'man. And when he heard the report of his death he wrote instantly to Madge to tell her to take no notice of it. He would like to see the nigger, or the crowd of niggers, who could kill such a man. But, all the same, though she was cheered by everyone save her mother, she Was now depressed to the point of despair. Grief and anxiety killed her red blood. She believed in the essential malignity of Fate' he was given and was taken away. When she kissed his photograph before she put it beneath her pillow tears rolled down her cheeks. She read his letters again and again, and slept with them in her hand. Oh, he was dead, he was dead She dreamt strange, incredible dreams, and was with him in the desert, and was with him in oases. She struggled through sand till it overwhelmed her. She dug him out of drifted sand. She came across his unmarked bones and knew them. He spoke to her. She woke with his voice in her ears and stared into the voiceless night. When she slept again she was for one hour happy. She woke again to feel his very lips on hers, and as the sensation faded she understood entire and utter , desolation. ! But she passed through the winter and came out of it alive, but languid and pale. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE CHAMPIONSHIP. Ah," cried Madge, "and an ounce of peace of mind is worth how much physic?" He might have prescribed relief from the com- pany of her .mother, for Mrs. Gretton was taking to society as some take to drink. To hide her own unhappiness she went everywhere, and made a thousand duties which did no one any good. Thus she tried to banish the intolerable sense of her own desolation ; thus she fought against that last flight from Egypt intosreligion, the last refuge of half the retired social world. She dragged Madge with her or attempted to drag her. She prescribed bright society for a broken heart, as if a waltz were a cure for a fractured leg. She prated of duty, and accentuated it by asking the faithful but sulky Maitland to dinner. He came, hankered, ntade eyes, was repulsed gently, and retired:with tears. l" Palace Gate became a whirlpool, a dance-house, a high-class gambling den. George was swept into his smoking-room and swept out of it by a lot of men he hardly knew, as they stood before his fire and smoked and stared through eye-glas es. Madge abhorred the Saturnalia, and smiled in a sickly way when the head witch, powdered to her scalp lock, cried high-pitched nothings to aliens and pumped social handshakes with affected delight at meeting some- one whom she had already seen five times that week and would see again. Mrs. Gretton was a fortune to manicurists, to massage fiends, to beautifiers. She fought desperately against the years, and by dint of nervous degradation believed she felt real pleasure in the unnatural dance of London life. Then Madge revolted utterly and took to her room, and went out alone or with her father. They often walked or rode for long silent hours. "Oh, when, when ? " cried Madge, desperately, and there was no answer to her prayers. But even so the time went on, and it was nearly eighteen months since Richard had gone. She knew the hour must be at band for good or evil fortune. He had promised to return before this. Even if he returned he must have suffered, and have met misfortune face to face. She sent her father again and again to the Intelligence Depart- ment, and when he came back he could not conceal the fact that Turner was growing anxious, nay, almost hopeless. But it was always in the hour when others did not hope that strength renewed itself in Madge. And now, though her father avoided her eyes, she lifted hers boldly. When first that ill report came she had changed her dress and adorned herself, and now she equalled her old resolution. She went no longer downcast, but seemed braver; so brave indeed that her father feared her—feared for her. He heard her attempt to sin', and as her voice tilled the room for a moment b 'fore it failed her, his eyes were blinded by sudden tears. She even went out again with her mother and faced the world, who knew something of her story, and dared to pity her who asknl no pity. One day in May her father brought home little Gwynne of the Goorkhas, who was in England on leave. He knew Richard and was welcome to her. He knew Billy, and was welcome to her mother. They petted the little ugly fiAting drrit all round, and made him relate bashfully '-how he got the Victoria Cross. At each men 'ion, and they were many, of Blundell 's name, Mrs. drettan winced. But Madge was proud and prouder of her hero. She looked at her mother curiously. What kind of woman was it who would not acknowledge him the equal of the greatest among living men? "N Gwynne, earnestly, "he'llcMomises hack kretstaofme e"nosuagidh. my men worshipped him. You know he led them when I was wounded. They think him a perfect demon, and will talk about him till they die. Madge could have kissed the whole regiment of Goorkhas as she wiped her cheeks. And that night there was a dinner-party, and Gwynne came in again for it, and found Sir Dan, now no longer Adjutant-General, but free to write to the papers and say how everyone was wrong in everything, after the manner of the relireelist. There was Annette, too, and Miss Fielding, and two be-diamoned dowagers like ambulant jeweller's shops of the most execrable and flamboyant taste; and two young men whom George Gretton hated. div.head: FINANCIAL REVIEW OF REVIEWS.
div.p: FINANCIAL REVIEW OF REVIEWS.

The Earl of Cardigan has been induced to break new ground by writing an article for this "Review." He deals with the question, " Can money be profitably invested in land ? " Mr. Stefan Muller, of the " Nene Freie Presse," the leading paper of Austria, writes on that nation's investments ; and Mr. W. Reeve Ennals contributes a carefully considered article on the " Forces which affect trade and industry." Dr. Henry Dyer, the well-known authority on matters Japanese, writes on " Legal aspects of foreign investments in Japan. Apart from these special articles there are reviewed a number of topics of interest, and not the least useful feature of this " Review "is the critical digest of companiee reports. Every important company known to the London and provincial stock markets is included in the voluminous up-to-date statistical record at the end of the volume, When we note that this record represents over a quarter of a million figures which have to be revised and published within a few days at the end of the month, the pablishers'may well claim to cover more completely this particular field than any other periodical or financial publication.

div.head: CHANGING SEATS IN A BOAT.
div.p: CHANGING SEATS IN A BOAT.

Four Liverpool cadets who are camping out at Chester hired a boat for a row on Wednesday and when near Heron Bridge they attempted to change seats. The boat capsized, and the occupants were left struggling in the water. Three managed to reach the side in safety, but a fourth young man, who belongs to *Seaforth, named Alfred Lovett, was drowned.

whose sole recommendation was their I'Vealth and (to some African tribes) their weight, put him out, for he loved beauty. The two young society men with atrophied brains and large eye-glasses annoyed him. The whole thing was a trivial jrj itne function. He yearnetil for a solitary chop and a whisky and soda. Mrs. Gretton, too, was well aware that the dinner was doomed to be as great a failure as her complexion. Her nerves were on a stretch; she found an excellent soup bad and tasteless. Madge would talk to nobody but Gwynne, and she knew they talked of Blundell. Maitland eyed his ally 'spitefully, and found no comfort anywhere. The hostess talked and said nothing, for ever, and having two or three subjects to avoid, led up to them by the irony of fate. All conversational roads were paths to India and Africa. To avoid the Charybdis of Blundell was to fall into the Scylla of Billy which brought up Gulistan, And again led to Africa. And, of course, as it stood, Gwynne knew nothing of the state of affairs in the family, and finding Madge only wanted to talk Blundell, it did not occur to him that others did not. He put his foot into it after the soup, and produced a big splash. "By the way," he said to Gretton, in a voice that was heard at the remotest boundary of the table, "I was talking about Blundell at the club this morning." "Yes," cried Gretton, not at all displeased. Indeed, he rather enjoyed seeing his wife and Fielding wince. "And there's not a man there, except some old, shelved pessimist, who doesn't believe he'll come back." , "Glad to hear it." "So delighted!" Seed Mrs. Gretton. • "But there's a queer story going round all the Service clubs about him," added Gwynne, who was pleased to find everyone attentive. • "Ahl What's that ? " asked Gretton. , Gwynne shook his head. 1 "We can't get it right, any of us. But it's how he came to be on Briggs's staff in the Gulistan affair. And I think perhaps you might know, as you all know him so well." "Oh!" said Madge, with a little gasp. / 1 / "It's about a telegram which was sent to Simla,' added Gwynne, eagerly; "and it seems that it was owing to this telegram, which was from the Secre- tary of State for War--" Maitland perked up. t "What From Pyichley ?" ! Is he the Secretary of State?" : "Of course!" said the disgusted Maitland. ' "Mr. Maitland is Lord Pytchley's private secretary," said Madge. "Oh, then perhaps Mr. Maitland knows about it?" cried Gwynne. 'About what ? " asked Maitland. "About the telegram which wasn't authentic." "Oh, this is very interesting," said Gretton, with an odd smile. "I don't know anything about it," grunted Maitland. "No more does anyone else," cried Gwynne, quite in his eery ; "but they say that someone in Eng- land sent it to the Commander-in-Chief in India, and then Blundell was taken from some dead-and- alive hole---" "Dum-Dum," said Maa,ge, in a clear, cold voice. "Oh, yes, of course,' nodded Gwynne; "and that's how he came to be in the Gulistan affair. But the oddest thing about it—and I'm sure you'll say it's very odd—is that Blundell himself doesn't know who did it, or how it came to be done." "Very remarkable!" said an eye-glass. "How romantic!" cried the first dowager. "How incredible But then truth is- stranger than fiction !" sighed the second dowager. She might well say so, being in society. They talked nervously, for no one but Gwynne was quite ignorant of the situation. Even he began to suspect something was not quite right. "However, when Blundell comes back, I'll ask • him. You've heard of this, Miss Gretton ?" he said, suddenly. She spoke with a vicious intent, and knew she set many nerves tingling. Everyone followed his lead, and asked some qaestion about the young gunner with a curious air of desperate interest. It seemed as if all the guests were over- whelmed with a desire to know the boy in detail, even to the colour of his hair. And Just as the atmosphere seemed clearine a little, there came at the house-door the double knock of a telegraph messenger. "Speaking of telegrams, there's another one," said Gwynne to Madge, and just then Madge caught her mother's eye, which she had hitherto avoided. But she now met it boldly, and there was a silent passage of arms between them. Interesting Presentation.

An interesting social gathering was held in the Buckley-street Independent Methodist Schools, on Monday, when Mr. J. T. Leach was made the recipient of a handsome marble timepiece on the occasion of his marriage. The present had been.subscribed for amongst the members of the church, Sunday school, band of hope and P.S.A., and was handed to Mr. Leach by Mr. Andrew Jennings, superintendent of the Zunday school.

. The prevalence of insomnia during the not season is mainly due to errors in diet affecting the organs of digestion and assimilation. Obviously the body has less need for heat-forming foods than in winter, and greater need for viands which tend to cleanse and cool the blood. div.head: VOTES FOR WOMEN.
div.p: VOTES FOR WOMEN.
Open-Air Meeting at Warrington.

A large crowd assembled at Bridge-foot on Sunday evening to hear addresses on the subject of" Votes for women." The meeting had been arranged under the auspices of the Independent Labour Party. Miss C. Pankhurst had been announced as the speaker and con- siderable regret was felt when it was known that she was unable to be present. Her place, however, was taken by Mrs. Mitchell, a lady guardian of Ashton- under-Lyne. The meeting was of a very orderly description, Mrs. Mitchell being accorded a patient hearing.___

COU;CiIIOT STOTT, who presided, said the subject before the meeting was not directly in their propa- ganda, but on behalf of the large majority of the Inde- pendent Labour Party, he could say it was one that had their entire sympathy. The subject of " Votes for Women "had been prominently before the people of the country during the last six or seven months. The members of the Women's Social and Political Union were unable to get definite promises from any candi- dates at the general election, but at the present time there were members of the House of Commons who, hai pledged themselves in favour of granting franchise to women on the same terms as men. That was what they were working for. He proposed the following resolu- tion :--" That this meeting of men and women of War- rington protests against the imprisonment of women who are agitating for political freedom, and calls upon the Government to enfranchise women without delay by inserting a clause to that effect in the Plural Voting Bill now before Parliament." (Applause). Mr. LUKE WELLINGS, in seconding, said he could not see that the women in the colonies who had votes were not better wives and mothers because they were enfranchised.

Mrs. MITCHELL delivered a vigorous address in sup- porting the resolution. She would apologise to no ode for being a suffragist. She would not apologise to the outsider or to the average man: she was only going to appeal to his good sense and good feeling. Some people wondered why they devoted their attentions to the Liberals, and in reply to that she would say that had the movement been started six months earlier, the Tories would have had a dose of it. (Lsughter.) Women should be enfranchised exactly the same as men. ' Did anyone think they were going to let young men have votes and their mothers, responsible householders per- haps, who had discharged the duty of citizenship sts bringing up those young men,left out without a voice in the government of their country! Her opinion was that had it not been for their agitation manhood suffrage would have been offered the country as the Liberal cry. If they did not get what they wanted from the Liberals,then the Conservatives would have to undergo a similar ordeal when they came into office. In this movement they had not gone down on their knees to ask men to help them. They had no need, for there were thousands of men in the country who were pre- pared to assist in the agitation. The Independent Labour Party programme contained as its first item "The equality of the sexes." Mrs. Mitchell went on speak of "sex bias." Women were ready to do any work but not to be degraded in doing it, and if any of. their work was necessary, such as the bringing up of children,they should receive honour for doing it. Just be - cause they were mothers they should be admitted to all the Councils in the land because of the children,but i t w those Councils. Ihse. y wTehreeymo askedtherswtohielye as should not enter idersaintoththaotlight the battle of life with bare lists. It was even noW pro posed that females should be excluded from faotoriez She would say that if this were done they would agitate for the State maintenance of married women. Taxes ot any kind were felt by women, who had no voice in the levying of them and they were affected by every Act of Parliament although they were not privileged to assist In their making. They were "far too low to vote the tax but not too low to pay," and aliens scoffed at English women because they (the aliens) had votes in England and the women of England had not. What was injustice for man was justice for women at the present day. With regard to the Education Bill, those who brought children into the world should surely have a voice as to how those children should be brought up. The speaker went on to refer to certain laws which she asserted were in need of alteration. By laws made and adminrstered by men,women felt they had decidedly got the worst of it so far as civilization had gone, but they were determined that the state of things should not continue much longer. They wished to be placed on a political equality with the men of the country. (Applause). The resolution was passed, there only being two dissentients, and the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to Mrs. Mitchell.

"Nothing. •.a nit nipped. sultry weather, I suppose. "You want waking up. What do you say to Looking in at a Soho gambling club? The show is worth a visit—once. Just to stir k it in the list a; things one ought to avoid, you know." Calverley was indifferent. Ali he knew was that he was not inclined for bed, so the two friencie walked along Oxford-street and turned into Soho- square. Gascoyne stopped opposite a quiet-loOking houss in grimy Greek:street. The street. door opened intc 'a small, square lobby, feebly lighted ; a partition covered with green baize formed the back of the lobby, (tad in the centre of the green baize door was an oval hole about the size of a man's heed. At a few words front Gescoyne whispered throng!) this hole, the door was opened by a dark, foreign- looking man, who, entered.t he names of the visitors in a book. They paid e small amount of money, which constituted them members wit hoot any ries or ceremony. they heard the sound of a pion-. as they ascended the staircase, and were shewn into a spacious nmin decorated and furnished quite in the foreign style—velvet loirges, mirrors, lace curtains and a good deal of tlirnished ornamenta- tion. The whole aspect was cheep r,nd. ii' dry. The company- matched its surroundings.' The dresses of the ,ladies had a decidedly sf•cond-hand look about them; the men might have passed rry well for waiters. •

Harold Calverley threw the telegram on the ,Ire,kfast-trible impatiently. He had to catch the reidnight train to Chatham, and he had looked 'or•eard to a long evening with Adrienne. He was feverish and uneasy. He could eat nothing. [be exciting events of the previous night were too 'resli in his mind. He opened the newspaper with •i Feeling of dread. Yes, there was an account of •I‘e police raid, but not a word about the dead in. Ought he not to give information to the golice ? But Gascoyne, it would injure him in his erofession; besides, he had given his promise not .o say a word. How the day yassed he did not quite know. 7":?ie .mly thing absolutely certain was that he ate little tnd had several brandies and sodas. Then he kept his appointment. The room into which Mrs. Verne 's maid ;hewed him was dark save at one end where the gale moonlight flooded the balcony. He could see the gracetui outline of Adrienne Verne's figure within the 01 en French windows. She looked dazzlingly fair in the pale mysterious light. The profile stood out sharp, clear and delicate against the sombre background of foliage, her bosom rose and fell in regular pulsations; the round shoulders were almost visible beneath the diaphanous gaga. of her summer dress. She turned her head towards him. A smile hovered over the coral lips. The long Inshes closed languorously, and then half-opened. "Dear, dear Harold," she murmured. Her words, the soft, enticing whisper, the glance front beneath those drooping lids, fired him. His blood coursed through his veins like liquid fire. "Tell me, Adrienne," he breathed, carried away by the impulse of the moment and the vehemenea of his passion, "do you love me?" • She snatched her lingers away, she covered her face with both hands; her bosom heaved con- vulsively. His arm went round her slender waist, and he drew her to him, trying to remove her hands. "Let me see your face," he whispered. "I want to read my fate there." Suddenly she changed her position, removed her hands, and looked at him. Her face was composed —niore composed than lie expected. "I am not like other women, remember. I shall worry you to death." I "Very well, then, I will die." A thrill passed over her ; he felt her almost tremble.

some of the members were waltzing to a piano •played by a little old grey-headed German, others were laughing and drinking., The air was tlr with tobacco smoke. Not a few cast a soniewhat suspicious glance at the two young men, whe certainly looked a little out of place in their fault- less evening attire and their unmistakable air of good breeding. - "Where's the gambling you were going to chew Est whispered Calverley. "Oh,' that's a floor higher. If this scene of revelry doesn't take you, we'll try the baccarat chamber."

Calverley was not sorry to quit the hot room, with its tinsel of gaiety, its fail-lost fetid atmosphere; and its polyglot sounds—n mixture of the harsh, tile shrill, the nasal and the guttural. They entered the griming saloon, where the silence, by contrast to the pandemonium of the room below, s,etred strange and unnatural. 'They approached the long table covered with green cloth unnoticed by the players who sat round. The latter were far to absorbed to•trouble themselves about anything save the cards and their chances. Yet the scene in a we!), was interesting, if only for the opportunity it afforded of studying the varied expressions of the gamesters.

"Do you promise to love me always—ever—until death ?" she persisted. "Until death and beyond." "That does not matter. There is no beyond," she returned, hastily. , They sat side by side, silent, for some little time, resigning themselves to the blissful, absorbing passion of a newly-found love. Was Harold Calverley happy ? He could scarcely say. He was infatuated with the witch-like beauty of the woman, but--well, there is often a good deal in that fatal but. Presently she raised her eyes, and those mystical orbs, now soft and languorous, travelled over the young man's face. "You have made me so happy, dearest Harold. Tell me now, when did you first love me ?" "How can I answer such a question, Adrienne," said he, in a tone of forced gaiety. "I do not know. I suppose I gradually grew to love you." "By degrees ? Ah, that-is not my way. With me I either love at once—or hate. I think directly I saw you I loved you. I could not help it. Kiss me, Harold. I want to know that you are there, that it is not a dream." _ . . . .

"I've talf a mind to try my luck, Calverley," whispered Garmoyne. • "Fools and their money are soon parted," was the sententious reply of his friend. "Never mind; the first seat that's vacant ... shall take."
The opportunity soon came. One man who was either tired or had lost all his money—Ahe latter, probably, to judge by his white lips and scowling brow—rose, and Oascoyne dropped into his chair.

At that moment a clap of thittider, one single, awful crash, shook the house, and for a moment the startled gamblers looked at each other in affright. But card-playing must go on though the heavens fall. The banker began dealing out the curds right and left, and the money was being staked when the door suddenly openNl and a swarthy- complexioned, dark-bearded man,his face twitching with excitement, rushed straight to the banker and whispered one word. That word was heard everyone in the room. "Police!" Instantly the men lerti*cl to ,their feet. One creepier gathered up the cards, the other tore off the green cloth, scarcely giving time to the gamblers to snatch their money._,
She spoke with a feverish intensity, every accent vibrating with passion. He kissed her. Her lips seemed to fasten upon his as though she wished to transfuse her nature with his.
"You do love me, darling, do you not F" "Yes, of course," "Of course," the echoed. "Ind are you happy —as I am ? "

I —To—GitscoY ne and Calverley the matter was very I serious. If the police took them into custody their Inames would be published and the scandal would be extremely unpleasant. Indeed, for a time, it would be Gascoyne's ruination. "Upstairs," whispered Calverley. "There's bound to be a trap-door. It's our only chance." It was a mad idea. but Calverley never stopped to think. All he wanted was to avoid the police. They dashed up a couple of flights of narrow stairs to the top landing. The glimmer of a gas- let shewed, as he expected, a trap-door and a ladder hanging on to a hook against the wall. In a twinkling the ladder was planted and the rusty bolts shot back with some difficulty. They replaced the trap-door and found thetuselves in a Loft, its floor thick with dirt and dust: A second trap had yet to be raised. At last they were on the roof, and, to go as far as Ihe corner of the next street was a very easy matter, for the roof formed two triangles running lengthwise with a gutter in the centre. Looking along the channel made by these triangles they could see that some of the houses had attic windows opening on the roof. "How are we going to get down exclaimed Gascoyne. "Phew There's a big drop of rain! We're in for a shower-bath. Pleasant, upon The words died away in his throat. A cu— rt cry with unmistakable horror in every vibration— burst upon their astonished ears. It was but one scream abruptly cut off, as it seemed. It did not die away naturally. They listened with beating hearts, but the sound was not repeated. What was there so agonising about that cry, so instinct WO an appeal for help, that made both min involuntarily think of murder ? Neither could say. Some three houses away was an attic window faintly lit up. Calverley could hardly say by wha, impulse he was actuated, but he ran to this window and looked through. A. vivid flash of lightning made the whole interior visible. "Heavens!" he cried. "Look at that!"

"I hope so." "You hope so. How coldly you speak I want you to be sure. I want you to feel that I love you with the only love that is worth anything—the love that makes a woman dare anything, do anything, stoop to anything to gain the heart she longs for. That is my love for you, Harold; cannot you understand ? "
Her voice sank almost to a murmur. He could feel her thrill with emotion. The lips, usually so crimson, were pallid, and, parting tremulously, chewed her small, white, even, strong teeth. . .

Harold Calverley left the house in a delirium of the senses which he did not attempt to analyse, nor could he had he so wished. Yet his intoxica- tion of bliss was dashed with shadows, not merely the misgivings as to what the General and his mother would say, but something darker, something absolutely indefinable. To add to his uneasiness he missed his train. There was no possibility of reaching Chatham before the morning. While standing irresolutely it occurred to him that Gascoyne's place was near Victoria. He would get, a shakedown there. Gascoyne, looking pale and wretched, received hint in a flurried manner. "It is as I suspected," said he, with some agita- tion. "That man was murdered—after the fashion of Thuggism. A handkerchief slipped round the neck and the thumbs ground into the windpipe, one each side. It was all over in half a minute. There's the evening paper—you can read all about it, for yourself." The dead man was named Philip Trafford. He had lodged in the house for some weeks, but no one knew anything about him. But this was not singular, for all the rest of the premises were let out for business purposes. Undoubtedly he had been strangled, but at present the whole affair was wrapped in mystery. "Unpleasant business, isn't it ? If I only had tbe pluck to speak, I fancy I could givr lbe police the clue," went on Gascoyne. "Look here. You remember my dropping my silk handkerchief and groping for it in the dark. I picked up this as well._l didn't find it, out until I got home."

The next moment he had opened the windows, which were hung like doors, and was in the room. A. second flash shewed a man lying stretched on the floor, his face congested, his eyes 'distended, his lips swollen. • - In an instant Gascoyne was by Calverley's side and was stooping over the body. "By Jove! muttered the surgeon. iead—strangled!" Amid the pattering of the rain was heard a significant sound in the adjoining room—the sound of a door closing softly. The two friends looked at each other. The same thought was in the minds of both—the murderer was making his escape. The two rooms communicated, and quick as thought they rushed in pursuit. An obstacle awaited them, the door leading to the landing was locked on the outside! "A pretty fix," muttered Gascoyne. "Locked in with a murdered man and no way of explaining our presence but that we were trying to escape the consequences of a police raid on a disreputable gambling club. Nice position for a rising surgeon!" • -• He took the silk handkerchief from his vest and mopped his forehead. The shock following the effects of the wine he had drunk had thoroughly unnerved him. Calverley, on the other hand, was perfectly cool. "Perhaps there is a way it into the passage Iro i the other room," he suggested. "Yes, yes," muttered Gascoyne, "I hope to goodness there is. Hang it, I've dropped my handkerchief."

. "That ! " almost shrieked Calverley. He turned ghastly white, and his eyes had in them an expression of unspeakable horror. It was the half of the silken scarf he had severed! The other half he had at that moment in his pocket as a sage d'amoir. "My dear fellow," exclaimed Gascoyne alarmed, "what ails you ? " "I'm going to take this scarf," he rejoined, fiercely. "Give it to me. I say." lie snatched the silken piece of gauze from the astonisl/ed surgeon's hand and thrust it into his pocket. "You can come with me, if you like," he went on, with it reckless laugh, "just to see I'm not. going to give you away to the police." "Wait outside," Calverley whispered hoarsely a kta little later. heir cab was at the door of the at where M Verne lived. "I shan't be long." Nor was he. ascoyne saw him come out of the doorway in a quarter of an hour's time staggering like a drunken man. The furgeon , had to assist him into the cab. 1
"The man's

"Would you like to know the solution of the mystery in Greek-street ?" he broke out, boister- ously. "I have just left the woman who strangled the man we found. He was her husband, and, Heaven help me! I thought I loved her, and only two hours ago asked her to marry me." He sank back in the corner of the cab and buriei. his face in his hands. He could say no more. But afterward, bit by bit, the story came out. Adrienne Verne undoubtedly was an adventuress, but, perhaps—who can say ?—not wholly bad. She had had a successful career as a Circe of the Atlantic-one of those fascinating women who find the great ocean greyhounds very profitable areas for their ingenuity whether in the way of robbery or blandishments. In an evil hour she married—married a man who was thoroughly vicious and who had done time. She betrayed him over some swindling transaction, he was sentenced to five years penal servitude, and he swore when he came out of prison he would pursue her to the ends of the earth and have his revenge. That note, delivered to Adrienne Verne late the previous evening, which contracted her face with a sudden spasm, told her that his vengeance was near.

Leaving his friend groping for his property Calverley hastened back. His conjecture as to a second door was right, and he called softly to his corntianion. "Found your handkerchief?" he whispered. "Yea, thank goodnegs. I dared not leave it behind with my name worked in the corner." They rapidly descended the Staircaie. The house was silent and dark. They met no one, they heard the sound of no one. Within a minute they were in the pelting rain and racing along the (boded streets.
"Please do set come \lntll nine o'clock.--
I

She was a bold and determined woman, and she did not hesitate. She hated and feared this man, Phillip Trafford, and she loved with all the force of her nature Harold Calverley. She went to the house in Greek-street. There was a stormy inter- view, but she, taking the man unawares, strangled him as skilfully as any Thug. And she used the half of the silken scarf to do it.

The next day Mrs. Verne's furnished flat wa, empty. The sudden death of a relative, she tole the agent, had called her away. Not a word di - Calverley or Gascoyne ever divulge, and the nayster. of Greek-street, so far as the police and the publa are concerned, remains a mystery to this day.

I "At Homes' are, as a rule, not very late func- tions. At ten the guests began to depart. At ' half-past only a handful remained. By a quarter to eleven the last man save Harold Calverley, was , shaking hands with the charming hostess. I Calverley, at the other end of the room, smoking ! a cigarette, was meditating over a leap in the dark. He was in the mood to propose to/Adrienne Verne and "face the music" of his outraged parents. The last man had said his adieux, and Adrienne was evidently about to come towardS him, when, the maid entered with a letter. Directly she took this letter in her hand he saw I a change go over her face, but it was only for a eminent. She broke open the envelope, read the letter, and, tearing it into fragments, threw it into the grate. When she approached him a smile wreathed her lips. "Adrienne," said he, with boyish impulsiveness, "how beautiful you look to-night!" "Don't tell me that," she returned, in a voice that was almost harsh. "Harold, I want to beg of t you a favour—go early, to please me. That sword business was too much for me. You thought I was ; iron-nerved. I wasn't. I felt horribly frightened." I "Do you really rant me to go? There's something I should like to say." "Another night," she returned, hurriedly. "To-morrow ? I have two days' leave." "Yes, to-morrow. Come to tea." He left her a little dashed in spirits. The evening had begun delightfully, it had ended dismally. He walked pensively into Park-lane. The night ' was intensely hot. It was fairly early, and there was no necessity to go direct to the Hotel Metropole, where he always put up when on his flying visits to London. . , By the time he reached Oxford-street it was nearly midnight. The last omnibuses were crawl- ing homewards, the horses plodding languidly along scarcely responding to the encouraging "click" of the •drivers. Suddenly he felt a hand laid on his shoulder. He turned and saw a man in evening-tiress and Inverness—George Gascoyne, an old college chum and now a surgeon. Gascoyne had been dining at his club and was somewhat elated. "What, Calverley, old boy! One would think you were .as melancholy as ' the drone Of a Lincolnshire bagpipe, ' as old jack Falstaff has it. What's cone wrong ? " . .

Glorious weather favoured the annual sports in con nection with the Warrington Football Club which were held on Monday. An excellent programme had been arranged and despite the counter attractions of the country and seaside resorts there was an excellent ring of spectators on the football ground, some 6,000 being in attendance. The proceedings started pudctuallly and the greatest interest was manifested in the different races. It is frequently a cause for complaint that at athletic meetings much time is lost between the events and the committee of the club are to be heartily con- gratulated upon the success which attended their efforts to prevent this. Another excellent idea which they adopted was in regard to the cycle races, To prevent ciawling they decided that the first in each of the heats and the second in the fastest heats should compete in the final, with the result that better times were recorded all round. Results :

150 Yards Scholars' Race Handicap (under 15 years of age).—lst prize, value £2 25., silver keyless lever watch, albert and seal ; 2nd prize, value £1 Is., oak- mounted ink stand and clock ; 3rd prize, value 10s. 6d., table gong ; 4th prize,value 55.. silver pencil case. Heat winners : J. H. Caldwell, Stockton Heath, 9 ; W. Rounds, St. James',lo ; A. Shepherd, St. James',scratch; S. Broadhurst, Parochial, 12 ; T. S. Green, St. James', ' 32 ;J. H. Kay, Heath Side, 9; A. Hughes, St. Ann's, 10; and A. Hatton, Heath Side, 11. The final produced a good race, a few inches only separating the competitors at the tape. Winners: I,J. H. Caldwell ; 2,W.Rounds; 3, A. Shepherd. 100 Yards Hanciicap.—lst prize, value £lO, ormolu clock and vases ; 2nd rize, value £3. silver-plated fruit and floNser stand; 3rd prize, value £l, silver-plated cake basket.. Heat winners : A. Sutton,Southport a.,

7 ; A. Smerdon, Sefton H., 7; A. E. Baker, Manchester ! T.A.C. 71.' A. Burgess. Salford H. 71; J. W. Scotland, Liverpool OM., 9.:1; F. Earley, Macclesfield H., ; T. Cook, Leigh A.C., 81; A. Brown, Swinton, 91. Semi- final : A. Smerdon, A. E. Baker' F. Earle, and A. Brown. In the final Smerdon and Brown ran a neck and neck race until a few yards from the tape when the Swinton man got a few inches ahead. A couple of feet separated Smerdon and Baker. Time, 9 4-ssecs. 220 Yards Handicap.—lst prize, value .£4, gent's solid gold albert ; 2nd prize, value £2, walnut bracket clock; 3rd prize, value £l, silver-plated celery dish. Heat winners : C. W'. Cole, Middlesboro'll ;T. A. Baldwin, Sheffield U.H., 121 ; S. Green, Salford IL, 161 ; J. ! Oakes, Warrington, 16 • J. E. Temple, North Shields, ' In the final Bald win made a splendid effort, but was beaten by four yards in the final sprint, the race falling to Green. Five yards separated Baldwin and Temple. Time 22 2-ssecs. One Mile Bicycle Novice Handicap.—lst prize, value £4, silver-plated tea set and oak-mounted tray ; 2nd prize, value £2, silver-plated fruit sugar and cream stand ; 3rd prize, value £l, cut glass and silver-plate claret jug. Heat winners: L. C. Daintith, Warringtan C.C., scratch ' • L. F. Wood, Warrington, 35 ; A. Cash, Bold, 5 ; H. flaslam, Bolton, 32 ; H. Mawdsley, Rixton, 40. The final was won by Mawdsley by four lengths ' after a hot race. A. Wheel gave Cash the 2nd place over ' Ila,lam. Time 2min. 45 2-ssecs.

600 Yards Obstacle.—lst prize, value £3, carved walnut barometer ; 2nd prize, value £l, silver-plated egg frame ; 3rd prize, value 10s., silver-plated sardine box. Heat winners : F. K. Merrison, Salford H., scratch ; S. Harrison, Warrington, 60 A. Ford, Warrington, 60 ' • H. Foster, Warrington,4o J. Stewart, Wallington H. 60; J. Bramhall, Warrington H. 60 ; H. BOyle, Warrington, 35 ; S. Kirkham, Cadjs. head, 70. Considerable amusement was occasioned in the final when the bridge was reached. Four men got over safely but the remainder, arriving in a body began to struggle to be first up the plank with the result that they were all put out of the running, winners 1, J. Stewart ; 2, A. Ford ; 3, J. Bramhall, won by two yards. Four yards separated the second and third, One Mile Bicycle Handicap.—ist. Prize, value £4, silver-plated revolving soup Tureen ; 2nd prize, value £2, Gents' Travelling Bag ; 3rd prize value £l, 6 bottle dinner cruet. Heat Winners : J. Houghton, Warrington, 120 ; J. G. Hall, Rotherham 182 • G. Franklin, Irvine C.C.,188 ;H. Wilson, Manche ' Manchester A.C. 168. In the final Wilson rode with great judgment and after being content with second place throughout,came to the front on the straight. Houghton followed closely but wat not able to overtake the leader who crossed the tape a length ahead. Two lengths separated Houghton and Hall. Time 2 mins. 41 4-5 secs. Two Miles Bicycle Handicap.—lst prize, value £l, case of fruit combination ; 2nd prize, value £2, oak mounted smoker's cabinet ; 3rd prize, value El, silver- plated tea pot. Heat winners : G. Dandy, Rixton, 290 ; A. Ackerley, Broadheath, 280; H. Wilson , Manchester A.C., 255 ; L. C. Daintith, Warrington C.C., 270 ; B. Gornall, Warrington, 220 ; J. Houghton, War- ' rington, 190. This race also fell to Wilson, who again won by a spurt when nearing the tape. Dandy was second with Ackerley third. Time, 6mlns. 6 4-ssecs. Two Miles Walking Handicap.—lst prize, value £3, silver-plated tea urn ; 2nd prize, value £l, silver-plated ' breakfast combination ; 3rd prize, value 10s., walnut timepiece. A good race was won by J. Yates, Prescot (380), who was twenty yards in front of A. H. Moore, Birkenhead (400). Price, of Warrington, who gave the winner two hundred yards start arrived a few yards behind Moore. _ .

' 440 Yards Handicap.—lst prize, value £4, quarter chiming clock and bronze ornaments ; 2nd prize, value £2, 6 bottle dinner cruet ; 3rd prize, value £l, silver- plated fruit dish. Heat winners: A. Burgess. Widnes, 34 ; T. A. Baldwin, Sheffield W. H.. 29 ; J. M. Nay, Pembroke H., 33: A. Smerdon, Sefton H., 27 ; J. Hicks, Liverpool 0. H., 33 ; G. NV. Ince, Farnworth. 19. The final produced an exciting finish, three competitors almost dead heating, Burgess broke the tape, but was disqualified for running inside the track, and the race was awarded to J. Hicks, with Ney second and Ince third. Time 49 1-secs.

SSO Yards Handicap.—lst prize, value £4 ; case of cutlery ; 2nd prize, value £2 ; silver-plated spirit kettle and stand ; 3rd prize, value £1 ; gents' dressing case. This race was run off in one heat and was won by 0. Sykes, Salford H. (20) ; with W. E. Kidd, Warrington (53) ; second and H. H. Fleetwood, Sefton H. (15) ; third. Tim, lmin. 55 2-ssec. One Mile Ilandicap.—lst prize, value £4 ; case of liquor combination ; 2nd prize, value £2 ; case of ' cutlery ; 3rd prize, value £1 ; case of carvers. This I event as usual concluded the sports and attracted thirty entries, twenty-four competitors turning out. The winn3rs of a good race were : 1, T. Turton, Widnes, W. H. 142 ; 2, T. Whalley, Warrington, 140 ; H. K. Jepson, Warrington A.C. 106. At the conclusion of the sports, the prizes were dis- tributed by Mrs.J.E.Warren,wife of the President of the club.

Throughout the afternoon the Borough Brass Band played selections on the ground, which added much to the enjoyment of the proceedings. The officials were:—Clerk of the course,Mr. T. Davies starter,Mr. T. Wainwright; judges, Messrs. J. Evans, T. Bowers,J. E. Warren and T. Locker; committee,Messrs. W. Hewitt, W. Chalmers, F. T. Barber, W. Nevins, T. Barnes. J. Dutton, F. lieesom, J. T. Bate, W. Hill, I Hackett. F. Turner, E. Gilbert, J. W. Evans and A. Jones; handicapper, Hr. H. N. Ellis; hon. treasurer, Mr. T. Pemberton; hon. secretary, Mr. IT. Ashur ; official judge for rycle events, Mr. E. Pickavance` ; assistant judge, Mr. A. Booth.

Dr. CLIFFORD, quoting "CHAOS AND Milton,describes the present OLD NIGHT." position of the Education question as "Chaos and old Night." Nothing could be much more apt. The whole of our Education controversies could be easily settled by a frank acceptance of the judg- ment delivered on Wednesday in the West Riding case. Local education authorities, it appears from this, are under no obligation to pay for denominational teaching. Mr. BALFOUR, by inadvertence, left something out of his Act that he undoubtedly intended to include. Local authorities may pay for denominational teaching if they liked to do so ; but if they are opposed to payments being made for such purposes there is nothing in the measure of 1902 to compel them to act against their convictions. It is rather staggering to consider that though two such com- Ipetent judges as the MASTER OF THE ROLLS and Mr. Justice FARWELL declare this to be the state of the law there have been more than 75,000 prosecutions under the contrary idea. In nearly 12,500 cases goods have been seized and put up to auction because, as it now appears, the owners did what they were perfectly entitled to do Passive Resisters have in the aggregate spent nearly 2,000 days in prison as a protest against the enforcement of a view of the law which now turns out to have been quite mistaken. It is an odd and I indeed, a grotesque situation of affairs. The old Ipersecution of sect by sect has been revived in the twentieth century under a total misapprehension of what was contained in a quite new Act of Parlia- ment,

There is further oddity in the fact that this prosecution may be continued. Not all County Councils are so enlightened as that of the West Riding of Yorkshiro. They may, in spite of the judgment of the Master of the Rolls, go on paying money for the teaching of the special d6gmas of sects. They are not compelled to do so, but there is nothing to prevent them doing so if they like. Passiveßesistance has been justified, but the reasons for it continue as before, except, , indeed, that they are greatly strengthened. It will now appear to the Passive Resister that he is required to do something that is not only repulsive to his conscience but contrary to law. If the denomi- nationalists were wise they would accept the judg- ment of the Court without further contest. For what does it amount to? It amounts only to an affirmation that if the Churches insist on the teaching of their specific dogmas they must do so at their own expense. Surely that is the real duty of Churches. What else do they exist for ? If they will not find the means necessary for the propagation of their own views, it is not unreason- able to think that they have no great belief in them The judgment will, of course, greatly influence the House of Lords in its dealings with the bill which it recently read for a second time. We doubt, however,whether it will influence that body in the right direction. What is most likely is that the Peers will take care to include in the new measure what was missed out of its predecessor. In that case they must again be reminded that this is a money matter, and that with money matters they have no concern. What is aimed at is the endowment of Church of England and Roman Catholic schools out of the pockets of Non- conformists. That is a financial question more than anything else. It is a quastion more directly affect- ing the rates than the Irish Labourers Bill, which the Lords were recently declared to be incapable of amending in the way they desired because there were certain provisions in the measure that might affect the rates by-and-bye. The judgment of the MASTER OF Tan ROLLS, supported as it is by so cool-headed a judge as Mr. JUSTICE FARWELL, Should suggest to their Lordships that it is really not worth while to get into a conflict with the House of Commons over a matter which is pro- bably outside their jurisdiction, and which, at any rate, is far from being in the position they sup- posed. Th 3 judgment in the Court of Appeal presents them with a great opportunity. In I legislating about the education of the child, why not leave dogma out of the question? Then, indeed, there would be an end of the reign of Chaos and old Night.
The result of the Cocker- COCKERMOUTH— mouth election has led, as AND AFTER, is only natural,to a demand

for the second ballot. In all those European countries which have to some extent based their political systems upon our own, the second ballot is regarded as a most necessary part of the Constitution. A Frenchman would not believe that he lived under a representative system at all if it were possible in France as among ourselves, for a member to be returned to the legislature by a minority of the votes recorded. The second ballot absolutely secures the representation of the majority, and there is no other way of doing this except by means of such a plan as is contained in a bill introduced to Parliament two or three weeks since. This measure proposes that, where there are more than two candidates before a single- member constituency, the elector shall be entitled to make two crosses on his voting paper, one notifying to which candidate he gives his vote in the first place, the other signifying to which of the candidates he would like his vote to go if none of those whose names are on the paper has secured, an absolute majority. Such a system would undoubtedly do away with the inconvenience of a second election coming close on the heels of the first ; but it is a remedy which appears to us to rely too much on the clarity of the ordinary understanding. It is probable that only a few hundred voters out of many thonsands would be cool enough,' ita the heat of a contested election, to mark such a voting-paper in the manner that would be exactly expressive of their wishes.

Our representative system is full of anomalies' all of which tend to throw the government of the country into the hands of a minority, as, in fact, sometimes happens. Not many years ago, the Conservatives had quite a respectable majority in the House of Commons, though the majority of the electors in the country had voted for their political opponents. The same thing [night happen though it is less likely, on the Liberal side. There is, first of all, the great inequality in the size of constituencies, which makes it possible to lose with more than 18,000 votes, or to win with less than two. Then there is our ridiculous system of registration, which, in one way or another, subjects thousands of other- wise well-qualified electors to periodical or per manent disfranchisement. The wrong of all this, which is bad enough, is deepened by such a con- dition of things as makes Sir John Randells mem- ber for Cockermouth and Mr. ARNOLD-FOSTER member for Croydon. If the condition of things which existed in some constituencies at the last General Election, and in the Cockerrnouth division the other day, had been much more general, we should now have had , the Conservative Party in power, though opinion would, nevertheless, have been quite as overwhelmingly in favour of a Liberal policy as, in fact, it proved to be. Thefact that our electoral system is an anomaly and is admitted to be so, makes forbearance and mutual accommodation necessary if the Govern- ment of the country is to be carried on by the party which has behind it the greater mass of popular support. It seems almost impertinent to make use of such a hoary truism as "United we stand, divided we fall," but this exactly describes what must happen in such circumstances as Cockermouth. The fact that there was only one Conservative candidate, whilst there were two candidates representing Liberalism and Labour made it absolutely certain that the seat would be won by the Conservatives. When Mr. SMILLIE came forward he at once made a I present of Cockermonth to Sir JOHN RANDELLS. He has done similar favours to the Conservative Party elsewhere.' He has fought six unsuccessful contests. He should now feel himself entitled to presume that there is no great public anxiety to return him to Parliament. Under a system of second ballot he might, of course, come forward as as often as he liked; he could do no harm. The majority would at least return its chosen repre- sentative on the second attempt. But, under the system that at present exists, candidates like Mr. SMILLIE are not merely a nuisance ; they defeat the purpose of the ballot, which is to secure the representation of the majority.
We are not pleased with the WHAT'S IN A Street Improvement Com- mittee's latest efforts at

nomenclature. By a recent resolution the new road leading from Wilderspool to the bridge over the Runcorn and Latchford Canal is to be called Loucher's-lane, while Chapel- street on the north side of Queen's Gardens is to be renamed Palmyra.square. If the committee wanted a really ugly and ill-sounding name for a new road they could hardly have advised anything 113arer the mark than " Loucher's-lane " unless they put an "S " before it. We suppose there must be some family connection, which could not be overlooked, between Loucher's-lane and Slutehers's-lane at Bank Quay 1 Then with regard to the Square—Palmyra Square. So far it has been a one-sided sort of affair. Now it will have two sides. Some day the Committee will learn that a square should flatly have four sides, and then Springfield-street and part of Bold.street will also be re-named.

The question of magisterial MioismarAL. appointments in and around APPOINTMENTS Warrington is one which ought to be taken in hand without further delay. Owing to the long reign of the Conservative party—a reign which has happily come to an end—there is almost every- where a preponderance of magistrates of Conser- vative political faith. We are sure most of our readers will admit that this is a national misfor- tune, which it is the duty of the Government to redress as far as possible. In Warrington the Tory 'Preponderance on the Bench is not very great, and of recent years the privilege ' which the local Tory leaders possessed has not been abused. Out of the thirty-five borough magistrates twenty are Conservatives and fifteen Liberal, but in the surrounding country district the disparity is much more marked. Here the Tories outnumber the Liberals by about four to one, and in common fairness to everybody there should be some readjustment. The Homo Secretary, Mr. Gladstone, has a conscientious man's objection to awarding magisterial honours as some return for political service, but never the- less it is only right that an effort should be made to get the names of a few more Liberal gentlemen added to the roll of the local and neighbouring magistracy.

of a week's holiday Suddenly the father heard a scream, and on looking round was horror stricken to find that both his wife and child had dis- appeared and the carriage door was open. Exactly how the accident happened is a mystery, but the most likely assumption is that the boy had been playing with the door handle and succeeded in , turning it, with the result that the door opened and he was precipitated on to the line. The dis- tracted mother leapt after him in a vain endeavour at rescue, and gave her life for her child who at present lies in the Infirmary. While the accident illustrates that there is undoubtedly danger attaching to inside carriage handles, it would hardly be fair to condemn the company,who adopt them simply for the convenience of the travelling public. Moreover,the handle.; do not generally yield without a fair amount of pressure. However watchful parents may he, it is not easy to keep children under control in railway carnages, but the terrible affair of Sunday shows that passengers cannot be too careful in this resplct. Tie victim of the second fatality was a cyclist who was making his way to Frodsham when he met a shocking end at Longford by children colliding with his machine and throwing him under a passing waggonette. The dangers which beset the cyclist through irresponsible youngsters careering wildly about the roads are well known to users of the highway, and the marvel is that there are not more accidents. It can hardly be expected that high-Epirited youngsters will realize the peril in which they place themselves and riders by frolicing in the roadways.

It is somewhat amusing to SLIPPERS AND "mere man " when he WEDDINGS, observes the scrupulous way in which certain cus- toms are carried out at marriage ceremonies by so-called up-to-date ladies of the smart set—who not only preach their equality but, in truth, dominate the modern household—to notice that no send-off of a newly-made bride is complete without the throwing of slippers. These are supposed to be cast for luck, but the custom originated in a different way. It is Oriental. In the East, every one on entering a house takes off his shoes so as not to spoil the carpets. There, where polygamy has been practised for ages,the harem often requires keeping in order, The handiest method of cor- recting a disturbance has always been the slipper. In some countries it is the custom of a bridegroom to place his slipper on the pillow of the nuptial bed as a token of dominion. In like manner, in cer- tain Jewish weddings, the bridegroom after the ceremony, puts a slipper on the neck of the bride. In the Bible, a man refused to marry his brother's widow, the latter asserted her independence of him (Dent. xxxv. 9) by "loosing his shoe." In llorocco, so much is the shoe regarded as an emblem of marital authority that a pair of richly- embroidered slippers are carried before the Sultan an State occasions, in the same way that one of the high officers of the household bears the Sword of State before King Edward VIL when he opens Parliament.

Both Lady Wimborne and THE EVANGELICAL Canon Hensley Henson FEAR, write in the "Nineteenth Century" this month on the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Church Discipline, and there is a singular agree- ment in the views they express of the dangers which the reforms suggested seem to them to involve. There is the fear that a revision of the rubrics in the direction of greater elasticity will admit some things under present conditions illegal, principal among which apparently is the use of vestments. Vestments are so undesir- able because, specifically, they represent doctrines which are inconsistent with the prin- ciples of the Reformation. They are bound up with Transubstantiation and the sacrificial office of the Mass. In the second place, there i danger in the reform of the ecclesiastical courts since the final appeal to a lay court in the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council stands for the supremacy of the Crown as against the tyranny of ancient ecclesiastical tribunals. But thousands of clergy already refuse to recognize its jurisdic- tion—what has it to do, they ask, with doctrinal and domestic affairs? "At every turn," "Yiss Canon Henson, "the High Churchman's clsira allowed. The craze for autonomy now carries before it in ecclesiastical circles," and the Canon last word is that any attempt to pass into law the latest recommendations of an ecclesiastical cora- mission will precipitate Disestablishment.

div.head: MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S BAND.
div.p: MESSRS. CROSFIELD'S BAND.
Mrs. Markel Gives a Garden Party.

enjoyed an immunity from serious holiday accidents but the August Bank Holiday of 190 G—one of the most successful on record to the thousands of pleasure seekers who basked in the glorious sunshine at seaside and rural haunts—has been marred by two fatalities of a particularly distressing character. The cir- cumstances of the awful occurrence on the railway near Acton Bridge which created a painful sensa- tion on Sunday afternoon are tragic in the extreme. Bent on making the most of a brief respite from toil a Hanley family were on their way to Blackpool, happy in the prospect

On Th -Ay afternoon Mrs. Markel gave a very successful "At Home" to which the managers of Messrs. Crosfield's and their wives were invited with a few personal friends. The party included in addition to representatives of the various departments, Miss Phipson of Harlesden, Miss Charlotte Markel of Darm- stadt, Mr. and Mrs. H. Roberts and Miss Roberts, Mrs Robert Garnett, Miss Jameson, Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Smethurst. The guests on arrival were received by Dr. and Mrs. Markel on the lawn. Afternoon tea was served in a large marquee, after which, the weather being exceptionally fine, the guests were able to enjoy under ideal conditions the music of Crosfleld's band. Indeed the immediate purposef,of the party was to give an opportunity to the staff of hearing the band before its departure for the French tour. Under the able conductorship of Mr. Halliwell a most delightful programme of some half-dozen pieces was charmingly rendered. So evenly high was the execution that it is almost impossible to select an item for special remark but perhaps the overture from the, " Poet and Peasant" gave the band its greatest oppor- tunity, and the horn solo in this was especially charm- ing. Another item which was particularly well received was the cornet solo, Millar's "Rave d'Amour." After the departure of the guests Dr. Markel expressed in a few words his thanks to the bandsmen for their services and congratulated Mr. Halliwell, the conductor, Mr. Bedforth,the bandmaster and the men generally on the marked improvement in their form which was so obvious even as compared with the high standard of last year that it had been a matter of general observa- tion among their guests. BANDSMEN'S SUPPER Subsequently the men were entertained to what is now their annual supper. At the close of the feast Dr. MARKEL seized the occasion to pay a tribute to Air. Mosso, to whose energy and constant devotion the band owed so much. He proposed they should all drink his very good health,and at the same time the success of the French visit. The proposal was taken up with enthusiasm.—ln response to general demand, Mr. Mosss appeared on the scene coatless, but wearing his blushing honours thick upon him.—ln acknowledging the ovation, he said he was proud of the band. Indeed he admitted he habitually spoke of it as "my band—(A Voice: "Cheek "and laughter)—and the truth was he regarded it so. He prophesied that the tour would be a great success, and they would return covered with glory. As for the fear Dr. Markel had expressed lest they should leave him (the speaker) behind in France, he asked them to dismiss it entirely ; they need have no apprehensions about himself. He did not mind telling them (the bandsmen) however, that he had written to the Chief Magistrate of Calais expressly enjoining him to keep his eye on them and to arrange for a proper police supervision from the moment they landed on the soil of France to the moment they quitted it. He had hopes in this way that he would succeed in bringing them all back with him, a matter which had caused him no little anxiety. The men spent the rest of a very pleasant evening in freely enjoying the surroundings and after giving a, most delightful, impromptu serenade left about 10 o'clock.
