div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present: Mr. G. Pilling, (presiding) Admiral Jones Parry, Messrs. T. Wright, S. Woodward, J. Hallows, R. Billington,G. Egerton IVarburton, H. Eyes, W. Weir, C. Roylance, J. Spruce, J. Whilly, A. Broom, J. Bolshaw, T. Guest, J. H. Davies, T. Antwis, E. Bretherton, C. E. Linaker, W. E. Hough (Assistant clerk) J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors) and J. Farrington (inspector).—Mr. H. G. Linaker was appainted clerk of works for the Walton Sewerage scheme at a salary of £2 10s. per week. RUNCORN AND WIDNES CO-OPERATIVE

SOCIETY. The annuta meeting of this society was held on Tues- day, Mr. W. E. Dudley presiding. The report of the directors showed that the sales for the half-year ended June 30th totalled £99,007, constituting a record in the history of the society. The amount was £3,360 above last half-year and .E 5,805 over the corresponding half- year. The net profit wa3 £14,818, and a dividend of lid, in the pound was recommended. The report and balance-sheet were adopted, and the dividend declared. It was stated that the new premises in Town ' Hall-square, Widnes, would cost about £lO,OOO when completed. BANK HOLIDAY AT WIDNES.

, Whines never presented a more animated appearance than it did on Monday. It seems strange to say "visitors to Widnes," but nevertheless it was crowded with them, the great attraction being the Transporter Bridge, which undoubtedly opens out the Cheshire resorts on holidays. Many Widnesians left the town for the seaside. Bus loads of pleasure-seekers passed through the town for Delamere, Frodsham, and elsewhere, via " The Bridge," The annual boat race for fishing boats took place in the morning, and owing to there being no wind the race was declared void. A scratch swimming race from the Transporter to Gandy's-yard was won by Charley Turner, of Warrington, Augues hccl Dickson, both of Widnes, being second and third. The Alexandra Theatre opened in the evening after the vacation with "The Indian Mutiny."

div.head: LABOUR CONTEST AT WIDNES.
div.p: LABOUR CONTEST AT WIDNES.

The leaders of the Independent Labour party at 1 Widnes have decided to make a bold bid for every seat' The vacancy in Waterloo Ward caused by the demise of Councillor Tom Laws is to be contested by Mr. Daniel Garghan, one of the leaders of the party. This action is being taken consequent upon the attitude of the authorities in refusing them permission to use Victoria square for their meetings. Wholesale prosecutions have taken place recently, and in all cases except two con- victions have resulted, including Mr. Seddon, M.P., and Mr. Standring, J.P., St. Helens. The ward is essentially a working mans ward. On Wednesday afternoon a deputation from Waterloo Ward waited upon Mr. John Winfield, licensee of the Railway and Commercial Hotel with a view to his standing for the Ward in opposition to Mr. Garghan. Mr. Winfield accepted. Both candi- dates are Roman Catholics, and as there is a preponder- ance of that body in the ward an interesting election will take place. RUNCORN LICENSING CHANGES.

At Runcorn, on Tuesday the following licences were transferred :—Mersey Vaults, Mersey-stret, from Adam Sutton to Wiliam Houghton ; Wilson's Hotel, Bridge- street, from Alfred Jones to William Hampson ,• Rail- way Hotel, Lowlands-road, from Stapleton H. Hughes to Thomas E. Egerton ; Brunswick Vaults, Brunswick. Street, from Charles B Pugh to Patrick Regan ; Water- man's Arms, from Richard Richardson to Alice Richard- son; Quarry Hotel, Weston, from John Nelson to Catherine Nelson.—Mr. J. W. Knowles on behalf of Messrs. Forshawt brewers, of Burtonwood, Warrington, applied for permission to alter the premises of the Mersey Vaults. Mr. Fred A. Lake, acting on behalf of Messrs. Peter Walker an d Co., brewers, applied for I permission to pujj down two cottages adjoining the ' Wheatsheaf Inn,'Bridge-street, and on the space thus 1 provided construct a sculley and form a backyard. The police had no objection, and the magistrates approved tha plans. In regard to Mersey Vaults, this matter was adjourned until Friday, so that the suggested alteration of a serving bar could be shown on the plans. BOWLING LEAGUE MATCHES. RUNCORN CLUB DISQUALIFIED. A great sensation has been caused in bowling circles in Runt:om and Widres by theodisqualificatio% of Run- corn Bowling Club from the Widnes and Runcorn League. The club is the premier club in the district, and was heading the league. A fortnight ago the first team met the Ball of Ditton Club at Ditton, and won eight games out of twelve and rumours of bribery arose. The League Committee appointed a commission of three members to make Inquiries and collect evidence. This commission has now made its report to the committee. The pro- ceedings were private, but the decision arrived at was that Runcorn Bowling Club should not be permitted to take any further part in league matches. This also dis- qualifies their second team, who were also leading, and were the probable winners of the silver medals. As there was no allegation against this team,much indigna- tion (says our correspondent) is expressed at this drastic action, and also at the fact that the members accused of bribery were not called upon to give evidence in defence. With Runcorn out of the way, Weston Voint are almost certain winners of Colonel W. Hall Walker's cup and the gold medals. MR. SEDDON, MP., FINED.

Mr. Seddon, M.P., and the Rev. Schofield Battersby, of Manchester, were among the defendants fined at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday for causing an obstruction in Victoria-square by addressing free-speech meetings. Mr. Seddon contended that there was a free passage, and horses . went by at a full trot. There had only been one case of complaint, and the gentleman who made that was very sorry. The square had been the meeting place for all parties for years, and the Mayor had held civic gatherings there. He was sorry, for the sake of public safety and peace,that the police had taken snob action. Politicians and lawyers of both parties in the House of Commons had told him that the prosecutions were either grotesque or malicious. Those proceedings had no terror for him, but he felt that he was bound to uphold the right of free speech.—The Bench fined him 2s. 6d. and costs.—Mr. Battersby contended that the case of Homer and Cadman did not apply to these proceedings, because in that case incon- venience and danger was caused to the public ; in this case neither was.—The Bench fined Mr. Battersby Is. and costs, and agreed to state a case for appeal.-- Many local defendants were also fined. RUNCORN BOARD. OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnighly meeting of the Runcorn Board of I Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present—Mr. T. Baxter (presiding), Admiral Jones Parry, Messrs. T. Wright, J. Douglas, G. Pilling, S. Woodward, J. Hallows, B. Billington, G. Egerton Warburton, H. Eyes, W. Weir, D. Roylance, J. Spruce, J. Whitley, A. Broome, J. Bolshaw, T. Guest, J. H. Davies, T. Antwis, If. Bretherton, C. E. LiMaker, W. E. Hough (assistant clerk)oW. R. de Prez, T. Cook and J. Pearson (relieving officers.)—The Finance Committee reported the payment, in out relief, to Mr. Cook .£70,1 Mr. de Pies £23 and Mr. Pearson IN.—The House Committee reported that arrangements had been I made for the sending of the children for a ' 'holiday in accordance with the accepted offer of Sir John Brunner. Some time past a little expense (7s.Gri.) was incurred for refreshments for an entertainment 1 party at the Workhouse. The committee recommended that the hat be passed round to raise that sum and that , the balance collected should be given to the children when they went to the seaside.—Mr. ‘Voodward sug- gested that they should wait until there was a full attendance of the Board before passing round the hat. —lt was decided to make a collection that day on behalf of the children and to make a levy upon the absent members to raise the 7s. 6d. The collection realized 20s. Gd. I.L.P. MEETINGS AT WIDNES.

Last Saturday week, Mr. Seddon, M.P., wired from Cockermouth to the Widnes I.L.P. :—" Party requires help for Smillie. Come next Saturday to face music. Police action scandalous." Consequently, on Saturday a large crowd anticipated his coming to address them. It was past eight o'clock when a wire came from him, saying that he had been detained in the house. It read :—" Parliamentary duties prevent presence. Have raised question in House to-day. Gladstone promises inquiry. Keep flag fly ng.'---SEDDON" The party decided not to go to the prohibited spot at the lamp, and several Warrington friends volunteered to address the meeting on the waste land behind the Technical School. The present policy is to report speakers who are bent on refusing their names and addresses, as in the cases last Sunday, merely rendering themselves open to arrest. The speaker on Sunday afternoon was a Leeds gentleman, who addressed a moderate attendance at the big lamp. Referring to free speech, he said that it was the sheet anchor of all their liberties, and if they gave it up, they might as well give up everything. The issue would not benefit Widnes alone, but the whole of the country. Personally he wouldnever ask permission of king, priest, or police to address his fellows. If they did, it tended to show that they had a right to be refused. They were becoming afraid of the Socialist party. The police were their servants and not their masters, and in some things they must be educated, and he hoped that at some future date the force would all bemembers of the I.L.P. No names were taken at this meeting.

Mr. Arnold Herbert, M.P., while driving with his wife and a lady friend in Wycombe on Wednesday night, was thrown to the ground and seriously injured through the horses attached to his brougham bolting and overturning the carriage. The ladies were not injured. At the time the member for South Bucks had his arm in a sling, having recently been badly hurt through being thrown from his horse.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 11, 1906. EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 11, 1906. EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

Bank Holiday. The weather on Monday was ideal from the point of view of the holidaymaker, and as a result there was a large exodus from Warrington to country and seaside resorts. -Blackpool was again the town most favoured and 700 Warringtonians found pleasure there. Six hundred journeyed by train to Frodslaam and Helsby to say nothing of the hundreds of cyclists who made their way in that direction, whilst some 350 went to Chester, Such places as Rhyl, Colwyn Bay, and Llandudno attracted 300 local excursionists, 200 journeyed to Lancaster and Windermere, and another 100 to Birmingham and Wolverhampton, whilst many hundreds spent the day at Liverpool and New Brighton and at Manchester. Practically the only local attraction was the Football Club sports, which drew to the Wildersp3ol enclosure a gay throng numbering over 6,000. Many spent some portion of the day in the country lanes in the vicinity of the town as a glance at the traffic returns for the cars will how. On the Waders- pool route 6576 passengers were carried the total receipts of £2B 2s. 91d. equalling 23.88 d per ca f mile travelled. div.head: EARLESTOWN CVESLEYAN DAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CVESLEYAN DAY SCHOOLS.

Miss Margaret Massey has successfully passed the County Council Pupil Teachers' Exhibition examina- tion; L. W. Owen and Gordon O. Finning have won junior exhibitions, and Florence A. Cutler also has been successful in the open junior exhibitions. Mr. Burgess and his staff are to be congratulated on the continued capturing of valuable exhibitions by their pupils.

div.head: MILITARY CHURCH PARADE.
div.p: MILITARY CHURCH PARADE.

There was great attraction at Ashton-in-Makerfield on Sunday afternoon on the occasion of the annual church parade of the A Squadron Lancashire Hussars Imperial Yeomanry at St.Thomas's Parish Church. The men mustered in good strength, and there were also contingents from St. Helens, Newton-le-Willows, and Ormskirk troops. The men marched to church headed by the regimental baud,in charge of Bandmaster Batley, and large crowds watched their progress. The Itev.J.ll. Bates conducted the service. A HOLIDAY EXODUS.

During this week Earlestowu has been remarkably quiet, for last (Friday) evening the employees at the Vulcan' Messrs. Vicars, and Messrs. Sleers works com- menced their holidays, and work will not be resumed until Monday, August 13th. The Viaduct works will be closed from Wednesday next until the following Mon- day. Both at the Vulcan and the Viaduct considerable activity prevails, overtime bar,' worked ; whilst at the Vulcan owing to the increased influx of orders it has been found urgently necessary to extend the htting and boiler shops, the forge and other departments. We learn that about half-a-dozen new steam hammers are to be put in the forge.

div.head: SEQUEL TO TILE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE MATCH.
div.p: SEQUEL TO TILE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE MATCH.

At the Manchester County Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. J. M. Yates, K.C., William Mackie (27), of Crow-lane, Earlestown, was charged with causing grievous bodily harm to William John Mason,Ladywell- terrace, Eccles. Mason arrived at the Old Trafford cricket ground early on Monday morning in order to witness the Lancashire and Yorkshire match, and made his way on to the" D "stand. On his arrival there he found that the spectators were passing away the time by throwing tomatoes, sandwiches and bananas, &c., about. This went on until about ten minutes past six, when Mackie received a banana at the back of his neck. This so enraged him that he looked around him for something to throw. Seeing a lemonade bottle close to him he picked it up and threw it at random among the crowd. It struck Mason on the head, cutting open his hat, and inflicting a wound on the forehead which bled freely. Mackie was arrested by the police and taken to the Old Trafford police station. When charged with the offence he pleaded guilty, and expressed regret at the occurrence and %aid he was quite prepared to pay compensation to Mason. Mason, after a short consultation with defendant, agreed to accept 5.:3, and the charge' was withdrawn.

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
YOUTH DROWNED AT ST. HELENS.

George Martin, aged eighteen, apprentice plumber, 43, Pitt-street, St. Helens, went for a walk on Sunday afternoon with three companions. The companions bathed in the canal at Black Brook. Martin took off his clothes and said that he would try to swim to the other side of the canal, but before reaching the opposite bank he sank and was drowned.

div.head: ST. HELENS GLASS BOTTLE TRADE.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS GLASS BOTTLE TRADE.

It is freely stated in St. Helens that there is shortly to be an important development iu the shape of a new glass bottle works at St. Helens. A new works is to be laid down at Parr for the manufacture of bottles. In the meantime it is stated that the demand for bottles is a good deal less than was anticipated considering the hot summer weather, and that two of the bottle houses at Messrs. Nuttall and Co., have been stopped, as well as one at Cannington, Shalv, and Co. This will mean that the employment of about 150 men will be inter- fered with, but for the past three or four years an arrangement has been in existence under which the work is distributed among all the men by a reduction of hours.

AST. HELENS MINISTER'S WEDDING. A large congregation assembled at Wesley Church, St. Helens, on Wednesday, on the occasion of the marriage of Miss Emily Bailey and the Rev. R. Johnson Cook. The families of both bride and bridegroom are very well known in the town, the bridegroom being a son of the late Mr. Robert Cook, and the bride a daughter of the late Mr. Mathias Bailey and of Mrs. Bailey, of Eccleston Park. The bridegroom has been stationed at Burslem, but the sphere of his ministerial duties has been transferred to Radcliffe. The service was choral, and the organist, Mr. A. Helsby, rendered an interesting programme of music. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. David Jones, superinten- tendent, assisted by the Rev. J. W. Hetherington. The bridesmaids were Miss Eunice Bailey, Miss Jones Colwyn Bay), and Miss Beryl Pennington.

div.head: ST. HELENS RECREATION FLOWER SHOW.
div.p: ST. HELENS RECREATION FLOWER SHOW.

The horticultural section of the St. Helens Recrea- tion Club has done excellent work during the past five years in spreading the love of cottage gardening and flower raising in window boxes; and the display at the fifth annnal show, held at Denton's Green on Saturday afternoon, was exceptionally good. Messrs. Archer, Threlfall and Finney were the judges, and the chief prize-winners were Messrs. P. Hitchin, J. Hitchin,,J. Clarke, E. Gavin, L. Fletcher, J. Anders, E. T. Lever and G. Forbes. In the cottagers' gardens competion the winners were H. Lawrenson ; 2, W. Owen ; 3, George Holt; and 4, John Sumner. Eight prizes were also awarded to other gardens for distinctive cultiva- tion. In connection with the flower show was a com- petitive exhibition of dogs, cats, ere. About 100 dogs were shown and prizes were won by H. Bradburn, J. Gilvray, Dr. Giles, W. Hardman, J. Stead, P. Cook, W. Evans, J. Pahy, H. Mercer, and S. Bagley. During the afternoon a new bowling green was opened by Colonel Richard Pilkington, who played the opening game with Colonel Lee Pllkington, both being presented with a new set of bowls. There was a large attendance, and he afternoon's proceedings were most enjoyable.
ST. HELENS MIDWIFE SENTENCED. "RELIC OF AN OLD SYSTEM."

At Liverpool Assizes, on Monday Ann Taylor OA midwife, was indicted on a charge of having, at St. Helens on June 9th, feloniously killed and slain Ruth Dinah Gibson. Mr. Lias prosecuted, and Mr. H. L. Riley defended. The evidence for the prosecution was that the deceased was the wife of James Gibson, a collier, and that the prisoner was a certificated midwife. The prisoner attended the deceased on her premature confinement. Twins were born, and both died two days later. It was alleged that the prisoner should have ' sent for a medical man and waited until his arrival, but this she failed to do. It was also alleged that she was under the influence of drink, that she unskilfully performed a delicate and dangerous ' operation on the deceased, which ought to have been done by a surgeon, and that she ceased attendance on . the deceased earlier than was allowed by the regula- tions. Mrs. Gibson's death was due to septic posioning, which was found upon a post-mortem examination to have been due to improper attention.—The witnesses for the prosecution included Dr. Buchan, medical officer I of health for St. Helens, who deposed that he explained to the prisoner her duties, which were set forth by the ; rules of the Central Midwives' Board, under the Mid- wives Act. The condition of the deceased, and the symptoms discovered at the post-mortem examination showed that she had not been properly trPatecl.--rhe prisoner, giving evidence on her own behalf, said she was a widow, and had been a midwife for thirty-four years. Mrs. Gibson was the only patient ant had died under her treatment, and there had been previously no complaint against her. She denied having been under the influence of drink at the time in question;_ she had not had any drink for about twelve months. She also denied having treated the deceased improperly. She I twice advised the deceased to geta doctor. Questioned by the Judge, the prisoner said at first that she had a clinical thermometer, but afterwards admitted that she ' did not know what a clinical thermometer was. What ' she meant was a small bottle of disinfectant.—Dr. J. S. Fox, of St. Helens, said that in his opinion, having heard the evidence, the case was a normal one as far as , external symptoms showed, and that he did not think 'it was obligatory on the prisoner to have called a doctor before that,was done.—Mr. Riley, on prisoner's behalf, submitted that at the most the prisoner had been guilty of an error of judgment, and not of criminal negligence.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and strongly recommended her to mercy on account of her age.—Bis Lordship said he would bear in mina the prisoner's age, the fact that she was a relic of an old system, and other favourable circumstances. She must go to prison for three months in the second division.

Salvation Army Festival at Allerton. ; For the second year in succession, the large field adjoining Allerton H 41.1 was very generously lent by Mr. Clarke for the annual festival and field day of the corps in the Liverpool district of the Salvation Army, and the event which took place on Monday was favoured with beautiful weather, in contrast vvito that which marked the occasion last August Monday. The celebrations marked the forty-first anniversary of the Salvation Army, and the Liverpool district cele- brated it in right royal fashion. Altogether there ; would be close upon 2,000 persons present, including representatives from nearly fifty different corps, sixteen of which were in the Liverpool district and four slum corps, while outside that area St Helens, Birkenhead, Warrington, Northwich, Seacombe, Oswestry, Wrexham' Chester, Thatto Heath, &c., were also represented. A feature of the day was the enter- tainment of nearly 1,000 children of the slums of Liverpool, who were given the outing and a substan- tial tea free of charge, and it is needless to add that the poor youngsters thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

div.head: INFERNO.
div.p: THE INFERNO.
[By M. H. Warmlll.l

Someetmonths ago I made casual reference to the meat packing business and to several side features not usually noted by the public, such as the breeding, feeding, and selling of cattle, sheep, pigs and goats in ' their transit to the packing houses, or places of slaughter. Since then I have been through one of these dreadful places and seen sights that made me I do considerable thinking. Ify first feeling was one of thankfulness that my wife was not with me; next, i could these men and women possibly be human beings or were they ghouls or vampires revelling in seas of blood? I had half determined to give to readers of the "Examiner" my impressions of this v'sit, but not feeling quite sure of myself, I thought it best to wait a little, and possibly a more experienced pen than I mine would take the matter up, and what is of still more importance, behind the pen there could easily be a keener eye in detecting the rascality that goes so far in helping the American "captains of industry" in making their millions of dollars. A Warrington I friend writing me just recently tells me that the impression he had after a visit to the States was that ! all was on a " rough and ready" scale. This descrip- tion scarcely covers the ground. "Rough and ready" within the factory walls, but none can deny that the goods, as exhibited for sale, appeal to the eye. They look neat and clean and the artist has done his best with the illustrations. But it is what we do not see , that we place on our tables as food, and it is to that, unfortunately, that the phrase " rough and ready " applies. I want to say right here at the beginning that my readers must not think for a moment that American meat packers are the only culprits whose murderous methods of making money are, or have been so far, successful. No you have them much nearer home, and will continue to have them, in all lines of business, so long as the present uncontrolled competitive qstem is allowed to prevail. Lest my readers should make the mistake of thanking God that they are not as other men are, let them read the recent report of the Inspector of London's meat isupply, and following that the report of the Inspector of Factories and Workshops and they will find conditions quite as revolting as anything to be found in America's "Inferno." In the report of a typical jam factory the inspector found "jam pots being washed in liquid like dark soup, which smelled abominably." The manager informed the inspector that the water was chang3cfabout 0000 a week. When fished out of these evil-smelling tanks, the pots were allowed to stand until dry, when they were considered to be ready to receive fresh instal- ments of preserves. Inspectors of bakeries found that it was a frequent custom to bathe the children in them after the close of work on Saturdays, and the family's weekly collection of dirty clothing was sorted in the bakeries for dispatch to the laundry. The sausage factories, says the report, are mostly owned by Germans, and are " small, dilapidated and, poorly lighted, and are infested by rats. So much for England's Inferno. On the occasion of my visit to one of these packing towns for there are quite a number of them I was first struck with the approaches and surroundings of the packing house. The site selected to build upon seemed tte have been at one time a big stretch of marshy swamp land, and part of the road and near the building lay over a tressle bridge that crossed a bubbling stagnant pool. A thought of rats might have Crossed one's mind here, but then, I had not at that time read the most famous book the twentieth century has as yet produced,—" The I jungle "—nor had I read the report of the Inspector of the sausage factories, so it was a case of ignorance being bliss. The yards around the buildings were clean, and there was evidence of plentiful supply of water being at hand. Further on I was shown the pumping machinery and the expensive and wonderful plant for filtering the water used. Let me say the water goes through a patented process that fits it for the supply of the boilers and the boilers never need cleaning out. Some of my readers will know this means a great deal in the way of cost. Before entering the Inferno' proper I was introduced to the office and a comfortable seat with a good cigar made one think of anything but stagnant pools ,and rats. Climbing the stairway seemed to give one a foretaste of what was coming. At the top of this four or five storeyed building we, found the hogs. With an occasional rest they had toiled up a passageway that led them into a corral from which there was no return They might kick and squeal, but the snout of each pig must move towards the wheel that carried the endless chain. Two men stand here, each with an end of the chain, and the sudden moyement of one of them catches a hind leg of the pig, and a similar movement of the other man catches the endless chain and away goes the pig and his squeal to the man, who, shod with rubber boots, and up to his knees in blood, slits his throat, and passes him to the next man who carries Vie slit down. another given distance. Oh ! the squealing shriek- ing noise, it was just fearful. Infernal seems almost too mild a term to apply to it, and it was then I was thankful that no member of my family was with me. The author of " The Jungle " describing a similar situation says : —" The men would look at each other laughing nervously, and the women would stand with hands clenched, and the blood rushing to their faces, and the tears starting in their eves." As the beast passes along, never stopping, he is cleaned out, and to each man is allotted his own particular part of the animal to attend to. Ultimately the chute is reached down which all goes and the scalding process is gone through. From the swinging up of the hog to the scalding vat, many strange things are clone. I say strange because I have no wish to be sensational, and the reader, or consumer if you like, may use other and stronger terms. Two meat inspectors stand, one on each side the chute, and as the animal goes by the verdict is given as to its fitness for food. If unfit label is stuck on it. I asked as to its ultimate destina- tion. It was condemned and goes to make fertilizers. As to this I cannot say, but a writer dealing with this point says :—" The people of —saw the Government inspectors, and they all took that to mean that they were protected from diseased meat. They did not understand that these inspectors had been appointed at the request of the packers, and that they were paid by the United States Govern- ment to certify that all the diseased meat was kept in the State. They had no authority beyond that ; for

the inspection of meat to be in the city and State the ! whole force consisted of three henchmen of the local , political machine! One of these, a physician, made , the discovery that the carcasses of steers which had been condemned as tubercular by the Government Inspectors, and which therefore contained ptomaines, which are deadly poisons, were left upon an open ' platform and carted away to be sold in the city, and so.he insisted that these carcasses be treated with an injection of Kerosene—and was ordered to resign the same week. There was said to be two thousand dollars a week hush-money from the tubercular steers alone ; and as much again front the hogs which had died of cholera on the trains; and which you might see any day being loaded and hauled away to make a fancy grade of lard. I might go on describing how old crippled and disease 3 cattle are bought up for canning purposes. How cattle are fed on whisky malt, and become what the men call" steerly"— which means covered with boils. How when the knife is plunged in they would burst and splash foul smelling stuff into the face, and when a man's sleeves were smeared with blood, and his hands steeped in it, how was he to wipe his face, or to clear his eyes so that he could see? It is an easy matter to drop a diseased beast into a vat, and the inspector to certify it has gone to the fertilizing department, but the vat may have a false bottom, and men may be ready to catch it, cut off its head and away it goes to make choice canned meat." In the packing house I visited, most of the work seemed to be carried on in dark dungeon-looking holes, and yet this could scarcely be so, as the building was many storeys high. I saw in some of these places mountains of frozen hearts and livers, all ready for export. In other places were the intestines beinai cleaned and packed for the sausage makers. I was told that the packed intestines, casings, were bound for Germany. In other rooms were large tanks of oil. All kinds of oil would doubtless come from these tanks. It would be interesting to know the history of a many of the drugs that cover the walls of a drug store. I do riot care to go deeper into this question,aud yet it seems to rue to be of such vital importance to the human race that it ought not to be looked upon\as a passing scare, and allowed to die out. Filth and vermin are closely associated with our food. Men and women work at this food and wealth producing business with a complete indiffer- ence as to whether they are spitting on it, or standing on it. I have just read a speech of Mr. Chamberlain's made at a meeting of the National Association of Sanatoria for workers suffering from tuberculosis in which he said "that more than 100,003 persons perished from con- sumption in England and Wales every year. If that were true, it was evident that this disease claimed more victims in the year than the deadliest campaign with which they were acquainted." When I read this I thought of the pancreats that were prepared at the packing houses, and passed by way of the drug store to the consumptive. Of late years consumption has became the " White Plague," and demands and is gaining wide attention, but why not start at what may he the root of the evil? Each town ought and must hive its own abbatoir and the question of profit must be taken out of the business. Remember that all our fancy lards come from those places and what goes in the making of lard is beyond me. Dr. F. T. Bond, Health Officer of the city, is in receipt of a letter from James B. Reynolds of the Pure Food Commission asking for additional information concernibg the "lard " which made several hundred children in the Good Templars' Orphan Home in this city very ill a few weeks ago. The lard in question was purchased from a San Francisco commission house.lnalysis by Dr. Bond showed that it was nothing more than a combination of. . beef suet and linseed oil. Dr. Band has sent a sample of the lard and a report of the case to the Washington authorities. The most strenuous efforts are now being made by the packers to put a stop to the strong feeling that the publication of the book "The Jungle " has raised throughout Europe and America. Newspapers are being floorled with costly advertisements in the hope that this will effectually gag the press, but if the White Plague is to be dealt with effectually, the food of the " workers " must be made pure. Ork of the most surprising features in an A.moricaa City to-day is the vasenumber of doctors there are ; and they are specialists at that. From the crown of the head to the sole of the feet, we, as a people, are all aches and pains. Take the following from cable from England. Bristol (Eng.) July 13. —The alleged adulteration of American leather was the principal topic of discus- sion at to-day's closing session of the yearly confer ence, of the Royal Sanitary Institute. Speakers averred that Great Britain imp nted from America in 1905 leather so impregnated with einem salts and glucose that the country paid 1.2),003d015, for what costa 45,000de15. The public health, it was added, I suffered owing to the fleasy shoes put on the market. I I have failed altogether in dojng justice to my subject., but it has not been from want of matter, but in sheer disgust. The above is bat a hint at a fear- ful scandal.
H. WHITIMI. 11

div.head: SOCIAL QUESTIONS AND
div.p: SOCIAL QUESTIONS AND
THEIR SOLUTIONS.
[BY W. R. LES UER, (Ex-President for the Scottish Lague for the Taxation of Lani Values). IL—THE UNEAIPLOVED PROBLENI. THE CAUSE.

Picture to ourselves an inexhaustible natural well providing free of cost a thud cap able of being fashioned by human labour into all those things which minister to desire—a fluid forming the raw material for all forms of finished articles-food, clothing, shelter or ornament in any form. To this well suppose that all men go to draw, and by varied processes of manufacture supply their wants as best they may. Bat sooner or later experience teaches them that this method of production is a tedious and wasteful one, as each man must be his own baker, tailor, builder, joiner, jeweller, &c., &c. So they hit on the plan of division or specialisation of labour, some confining themselves to drawing the raw material from the well, while others specialise in various Mimes. The former now hand to the latter the raw material they have drawn, and in exchange receive an equivalent value in whatever finished product they may want. here we have perfectly free and natural conditions in which no man can possibly extort fro .n another greater value than he'gives in exchange. The reward of each is in strict propqrtion to his product, the more active and industrioos reaping the greater reward—i.e.,getting the better wage—in measure with his useful activity. Moreover, no man willing to work could possibly remain i unemployed or penniless n such a community, because the well provides enough raw material for all wants and is freely accessible to all. Competition under such conditions is beneficial to all, because it is free And on I equal terms. It can hurt no one. Under such conditions nothing can be gut by one individual at another's I expense. In other words, free competition like this , secures to each individual the full products of his labour. All standing on an equality.as regards nature's free gifts, each man has as good a chance of satisfying his wants as his neighbour has, and the result to each is wholly dependent on how he avails himself of his oppor- tunity. Competition, it will be seen, in such circum- stances draws out of each the best he is capable of. It spurs him on to be of use not only to himself, but to society as well—i.e. it makes of him a good social animal. And now see how competition would work in preventing over-charge by any section of this free community. Picture, for instance, the manufacturing section endeavouring to overcharge the drawers of raw material by forming a ring or cornbide in manufactured goods. Is it not evident that rather than submit to the exaction the latter would start manufacturing them- I selves? If, on the other hand, the drawers of raw material sought to over-ottarge for their services, the manufacturers would promptly find redress in setting to draw the raw material for themselves. No ring or combine could be of any effect under conditions of freedom like these. Reward mast be strictly pro- portional to the value of services rendered. 90 that as advance in civilisation and the arts of production mean greater product, they would in such a society of necessity mean higher wage. Butnow change the picture. Suppose that a section of the community acquires exclusive possession of the well, so that they have power to charge the rest for access to it. At once this simple fact brings a .pro- found change over the whole structure of that society. Those who were before drawing the raw material, working it into finished articles and getting the whole product of their labour are now called upon to yield a portion of it to people who simply levy tribute, i.e., give nothing in exchange. They only give leave to use what was already there had they never been born—the well. Many are now unable to employ themselves because they must make terms with the privileged, well-owning class before they can get access to the raw material. They are thus reduced to the keenest com- petition for employment, where before employment came as a matter of course, just as it did to Crusoe on his island. Instead of coming naturally as it used to employment is now looked on as a favour, for men are bidding against each other for the right to work. Competition, instead of securing to each his full pro- duct and spurring each to his best endeavour, as it did before, now becomes a terrible scourge. For having no alternative of self-employment as they used to have, it drives men to accept a mere living wage and any improved means of drawing the raw material from the

1 well or working it into finished articles, instead of going to increase wages as it did before now only enables the well owners to extract the higher rent, because the more productive labour becomes the more does competition drive workers to offer for the favour of getting work at all. In this way the gap between rich and poor ever 1 widens, the well-owners appropriating a larger and I larger share of the total product in measure as improve- ments are made in methods of productior, while the non-well-owners remain at or about subsistence point. And more than this. It is easy to imagine the well- owners turning progress in the arts of production to their exclusive advantage in a very spacial way, for they would soon see that by putting a limit on the amount drawn from the well they could later on (owg to , the improvement being made) get a higher rent for what was left. This restriction would forthwith give rise to-- an unemployed class among the non-well-owner; who would compete for the boon of employment more keenly than ever, and so depress wages everywhere. For the supply of labour would always exceed the demand so long as an artificial limit was pat on the amount allowed to be drawo from the well. In this way work would, become so arca, and unemployment, low wages and want, with all their degrading accompaniments, matters of course And finding there was not eaough work to go round. we can imagine kind hearted persons coming forward I with their remedies for unemployment and distress. 1 Some would declare the ctantr9 to be over-populated, and produce schemes for s 'Japing some of the would-be 1 workers off to the Colonies ; others would demand 'checks on alien im nigration or on the size of families. Then there would be schemes for providing old-age pensions at the public expanse for people whose wage was now too low to pension themselves ; for municipal housing of the working classes—they being now too poor to decently house themselves ; for a minimum wage to the workers—whose wages, if they earns by their own, would be far above a minimum. Others would declare that the cause of poverty was too much drink or too little thrift. Then habits and customs would come under criticism, and the poor proincers would be told that they attended too many football matches of a Saturday or that they kept their beds of a Sunday (after a six days of monotonous and under- paid toil.) . .

And so the mockery would go on, while the few who might suggest that the real remedy for all the trouble was for the community to revert to free conditions by overthrowing monopoly in well ownership, and thus allowing every man equal right of access to the well, would be branded as attackers on the "sacred rights of property" and confiscators of the most dangerous kind. Need we talk longer in parable? Substitute "land' for "well," and the conditions above pictured broadly correspond with social conditions as they actually exist in all civilised countries to-day. Land, which is the source of all wealth, and without which no man can live, was once, like the well, common property, but has in all civilised states become more or less monopolised by the few, who charge the rest for its use. The fact that there are many landlords, and not one only does not alter the situation, for as J. S. Mill has shown, "a thing which is strictly limited in quantity, even though its possessors do not act in concert, is still a monopo- lised article." In the history of all races men at one time had equal rights to use land, and wherever nature was fairly propitious, there neither poverty on the one hand nor great wealth on the other was to be found, and that remains true of those primitive communities where land is still held in common. Wealth there is well distributed, and men are inure their own masters than in highly civilized states where all land is monopolised. They are dependent on no one for a living. Such " backward" people who have maintained equal rights to land have little to envy Europe or America, where legions are either unemployed, over- worked, or living in constant dread of want. The effects of land monopoly may perhaps bast be ' seen in the United States of America, whosq history is short, though they are evident in all civilised states. Not many generations past land could be had for the asking, for then there were no speculating companies or individuals to forestall the settlerand demia3 rent or perchance entirely prevent present settlement, as there are to-day. Though few of the present marvellous I aids to labour were then available wellbeing was very general and wages high where nine worked for wages. The keen-eyed de Toqueville in recording his impres- sions states that he was struck more than anything • else by the genera equality and prosperity then pre- vailing. "The truth is," said Benjamin Franklin "that though there are in that country but few people so miserable as the poor of Europe, there are also very few that in Europe wofild be called very rich. There are few great proprietors and few tenants." In 1793 the richest man in America was reputed to be John Flaycock and he was worth £70.000. He was quite outstanding,. On the other hind chronic or deep ipoverty wages unknown as great wealth, and the reason I is plain. The easy access to land made it comparatively simple for all men to get subsistence, and because it was so easy for men to employ themselves wages were necessarily high. Whenever they were dissatisfied with the wages'obtained by following trades, or in working for others, " thee could," as Thomas Jefferson said, " Quit such vocations, take up some land, and go labouring the earth' for themselves."

Mr. James Bryce observes that to the twenti there were no great fortunes in America and no povertY- " But now," he says, "there is some poverty, and a greater number of gigantic fortunes than anywhere else in the world." And why? Is it not because, as T. G. Shearman declared in 18S0, the United States is prim- ticelly owned by 230,000 people, and if the concentrat- ing movement continues, will very soon be substantially owned by 50,030 persons ? The same movement has for long been apparent in Great Britain. Professor J. E. Thorold Rogers, in his "Six Centuries of Work and Wages," says that "in 1495 a peasant could provision his family for a twelvemonth with three-quarters of wheat, three of malt, and two of oatmeal by fifteen weeks' ordinary work ; an artisan could achieve the same result in ten weeks." Some forty years later it was not secured as the result of twelve months' wprk. what had happened to cause this change? In the year 1509 began the robbery of the commons from the labourers. The commons were forcibly parcelled out as private property among landlords, and the people rack-rented for them. On page 355 he states that though "the mass of English working men are far better off now than they were two generations ago, yet, relatively sneekinc, the working man of to-day is not so well oft as he was in the fifteenth century." People to-day have either too much or not enough work. Or take the testimony of Sir Henry Maine, the great jurist, in his " Village Communities " :—" The terrible problem of pauperism began to press on English states- men as soon as the old English cultivating groups (in which land was collectively and not privately owned) began distinctly to fall to pieces." To-day society is oppressed by the spectre of "the unemployed," whose number in this country is variably estimated in average times at from 500,000,t0 1,200,000 Land speculation,i.e., the withholding of land from use in expectation of a rise in its value, is undoubtedly the main cause of unemployment. This practice is very general in all growing communities. As industry cannot be pursued, or men fan employment in any capacity whatever with- vent in some way making use of land, it follows that unemployment is general in proportion as the practice is in vogue of speculatively withholding land from use. It is estimated that in Great Britain since 1870. 7,000,000 acres have either gone out of use altogether or have been put to inferior uses, and that since the same date 1.000,000 fewer men are employed in the rural districts. The Royal Commission on the Housing of the Working classes, 1333, specially condemned the practice of speculators withholding land,and largely attributed bad housing and high rents to it. Henry George in "Pro. gess and Poverty" went to the root of the matter when he wrote "Did we ever think what a strange thine it is that men cannot find employment 0 lf men cannot find employment why cannot they employ them- selves ? Simply because they are shut out from the element on which human labour can alone be exerted, Men are compelled to compote with each other for the wages of an employer because they have been robbed of the ,paturat opportunities or employing themselves ; because they cannot find a piece of God's world to work on without paying some other ham In creature for the privilege." Unused land means unemployed men. The land ques- tion and the unemployed question are really offe. If the land of Britain were as productively used as is the land of Belgium hundreds of thousands would find employment who are now driven to the alternative of idleness or emigration. Take as a concrete case an estate of 300 acres in Surrey which was recently bought by a co-operative small holdings society. it was cut up into sixty holdings of five acres each and advertised for sale on fair terms. There was a great demand for tho holdings, and when settled there were established at work sixty families, where previously there were only three. Notice how the question of unemployment came in here. First we have sixty families employed where preciously there were only three, and secondly these sixty families now send their produce to the towns and get in exchange articles of all kinds, snob as clothing furniture, literature, building material, etc., which are made in the towns. They thus help to increase the demand for labour, and afford employment in the towns. They having got apcess to land in the country not only employ themselves but give employment to city workers previously i workless, per- haps, hundreds of miles away. The interests of the towns are bound up with those of the country. We see here how beautiful is the action of natural law. In working productively for himself no individnal can fail to work for others also, and the more he does for himself the more he does for others. Hence, any institution which stands in the way of employment has results which reach far beyond the individuals imme- diately affected. The central fact to hold firmly to is that even in the most complex society such as ours men cannot find employment without using land in some form and that unemployed acres mean unemployed men. i If we think out why it s that multitudes of the " sons of men 'shave no where to lay their heads, or even are deprived of bread to eat, we shall find that the hiring out of land by private parsons, and the holding af it up for a rise in value is at the bottom of it. If this is true it seems clear that we most first deal with the land question if we are ever to be in a position to tackle effectively and permanently the questions of unemploy- ment, housing and poverty. We shall next enquire what Socialism has to offer as a solution of any of these problems.
(To be continued).

div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
PRETTIEST HAT.
The sun-bonnet made of gingham or cambris is certainly the prettiest possible frame for a laughing little baby face.
It shews the sunny curls clustering about the temples so charmingly, and those that escape at the back of the quaint little frills, points out a contemporary, that are a feature of the bonnet.

div.head: ATTRACTTVE WOMANHOOD.
div.p: ATTRACTTVE WOMANHOOD.

No womiin need be ugly. If there is a soul in her body, it has but to begin sometimes to ishew through. From her earliest girlhood the thought she thinks, the feelings to which she Fives way, the tones she utters, the wishes she Indulges, are sculpturing lines in her face which are capable of making a beauty all her own— lines the writing of which will remain when bloom fades. and spa ride fails. It is in the be. %ginning of manhood and in the beginning of old age that a man is captivated simply by a pretty face, and is in breathless haste to make her charms his own possession. The mature man is far less subject to a mistaken infatuation. The boy looks for beauty, the glowing cheek, the melting eye, the lovely lip; he cannot endure the notion he will say, of an unlovely counten- ance in perpetual evidence. A USEFUL ADJUNCT.

The subject of our illustration is a useful wrap that will serve its owner on dozens of occasions during the summer and autumn. It is a slack coat, single-breasted, and having a couple of pleats over each shoulder and corresponding' ones down the back, which arc held in place by a strap placed across the waist line. The sleeves are full and capelike, and are finished with a strap

tap of the arm matching that on the back of tne coat, so that when desired, the full- banging part of the sleeve can be drawn up close .to the arm by means of this strap, which is sup- plied with a button and buttonhole. Almost any material with a rain-proof finish is suitable for this coat, and as some of these are made with a fancy back no lining will be necessary unless it is added for warmth.
THE SILENT NURSERY.
Since she first ascended the throne the young

Queen of Holland has never had reason to doubt for a moment that she is one of the most popu- lar of European Royalties. In the delicate and tender sympathy which has been almost uni- versally shown during the last few days in the disappointment of her hopes, she has had ample evidence that the affection of European peoples for her is an abiding affection. She is our little Queen of Peace. It is to her pretty, unpreten- tious home in the woods at The Hague that the nations repair when they discuss how best to fashion ploughshares from swords, and pruning- hooks from spears. Practically all peoples, nations, and languages were represented in that famous Conference in the Orange Room at the Huis. Ten Bosche. and as many will be there next year, to seek, in the peaceful atmosphere of her summer home, the key to the millen- nium. Hence she is a wotld 4ure in mor, qema the aanse that
nolTand, and as snob The object of worIT-Wide solicitude.
A NEW SHIRT.

The subject of our illustration is a very neat and smart little morning shirt suitable for early- autumn wear. The material of which it is made is a pretty pale-blue viyella, patterned with an almost invisible stripe of white. The top of the blouse is arranged with a deep tabbed yoke, machine-stitched round the edges, and finished

with groom ot little white buttons. On to the yoke the lower past of the blouse is gathered with a fair amount of fulness, which is allowed to pouth slightly over the deep plain waistband. Down the middle of the front runs a plain box- pleat, machine-stitched at the edges, and further adorned with groups of hi:Co white buttons. The sleeves are of the small bishop shape, and are finished with neat little tabbed cuffs, stitched and buttoned to match the yoke. A turn-down collar and jaunty little silk stock complete this smart and becoming shirt.

div.head: WOMEN'S LOT IN MONTENEGRO.
div.p: WOMEN'S LOT IN MONTENEGRO.

Sir Herbert Maxwell has an interesting article on Montenegro in Blackwood. Contrasting the 'omen of the country, in which the men are of a particularly fine physique, the writer says: The plain fact is that the lot of women in this Christian country is far harder than that of Mussulman wives who are kept in seclusion. The Greek Church, despite its veneration for the Virgin Mary, has done little or nothing to modify the Oriental doctrine of the abject in- feriority of woman to man. Consequently, all the burdensome tasks are thrown upon women, except agriculture and wood-cutting, which they share with the men. But even that share is not an equal one. If a man goes to the copse to cut firewood, it is his wife who binds the load and' carries it home, over the steep paths, on her shoulders. A family attending market always marches in the same order. The remark that "it is not from unkindness . . . it is simply the constituted order of things that man is the rd" recalls the well-worn saying that more sins are committed from thoughtlessness than from wickedness. TO-DAY'S RECIPS.

MUFFIN Es.—Slit two muffins round the edges, taking care not to cut them right through, and toast them in the usual manner on both sides. Pull them open and spread them plenti- fully with butter, and place in the oven to keep warm. Then prepare a sauce in the following manner: Take the yolks of two eggs, beat them well, and add a very little flour and a small piece of butter. Season with pepper,. salt, one dessert- spoonful of vinegar and two or water. Place is a cup and stand it in a saucepan of fast-boiling water. our tin tile sauce tnicsens, out remove before it comes to the boil. Add a small piece of butter, and stir till it melts. Poach four eggs, place them on the muffins, and pour the sauce *ver them Serve immediately.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

A meeting of this Society was held on Sunday last in the Winwick-street Co-operative Hall, when Mr. R. Atkinson the hon. treasurer presided and spoke upon the old adage A Sabbath well spent, brings a week of content." While those words are not found in the Bible, yet they bore out, he said, the spirit of the Bible. The happy Sabbath thoughts,Sabbath services, with the peaceful moments, and loving reflections gave tone, spirit and energy for the duties of the week. The experience of those happy meetings,made them stronger for the duties of life, and gave them influence for good over their fellows. Mr. J.Ewan, of Sale, was the speaker, and spoke upon, "All things work together for God, to them that love God." Paul knew what he was talking about. We naturally followed the advice of older men, and men who know, and who had passed through the mill. Paul though not an old man, yet was old in great experiences. His own lot had been hard and rough, yet it ended in his eternal good. He presented sound character, timely wisdom, and good advice to his fellows, then his end was Christ and eternal gain. Miss A. Griffiths sang "The promise of life" and was greatly appreciated. Mr. W. Pearce presided at the piano. Mr. D. Owen and Mr. Joseph Garner also took part in the meeting. The Secretary announced that £1 2s. 6d. was received for the Organ Fund, and that the Savings Club would open next Sunday.

Bridget Morgan appeared in the dock at the Warring- ton Police Court on Wednesday charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road. This was her eighty-second appearance. The magistrates imposed a fine of 20s. and costs, or one month, and as she left the dock she bad the chairman a polite "good morning."

The Warrington " Examiner " is now published on i Friday afternoon, price one penny, and s on sale at the various newsagents at about 4 o'clock. Should any difficulty be experienced in getting the paper the proprietors will undertake to deliver a copy at any I address in Warrington by 5 o'clock on Friday after- noon without extra charge. Address all communica, tions to" Examiner Office," Bewsey-street Warrington Will of Mr. John Clowes Sutton. The will of Mr. John Clowes Sutton, of Market-st., Warrington, and of Stockton Heath, furnishing draper, who died on the 21st June last, has been proved at £2,048, Ship Canal Mosquitoes. , • Mosquitoes have made their appearance in the villages bordering the Ship Canal between Man- chestexind Warrington. Numerous residents have complained of the bites from the insects, which are supposed to have been brought up the canal in timber boats from foreign countries. STILL LEADING, the "HERALD" KITCHEN RANGES and " PEVERIL " FIRE GRATES Sole Agent.—J. S. I GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge-at., Warrington,—Advt. Guardians' Vacancy.—Mr. Whittle Withdraws. On Tuesday Mr. F. J. Whittle withdrew his candi- dature in favour of Mr. W. C. Brooks, for the seat rendered vacant by the Rev. Father Mercer in the representation of St. John's Ward on the Board of Guardians. Mr. Brooks is therefore returned unopposed. Warrington and the Foresters. At the Foresters' High Court at Ling's Lynn on Tues- daY Northampton was chosen for the High Court of 1908 receiving 450 votes, Birmingham 77, Swansea 77, Glasgow 38, Burton 24, Belfast 15, Chatham 15, and Warrington 7. The Warrington Foresters are desirous that the Court should be held at Warrington and will continue to advocate their claim until their objet is achieved.

"I tried it to-day at school when Willie Ander- son hit me, and before I got to three he'd hit me again. Then I began all over again, and jUst as I got to six he gave me another under the ear." `You should count by tens, m 9 boy," said Archie's big brother. A sergeant who was trying to lick into shape a dozen of the rawest of raw recruits, must have felt a good deal embarrassed by the unexpected turns which things took. One morning, having marched the men out to the drill,ground, he proceeded with the customary business. "Eyes right!" sounded from the sergeant's husky throat. "So's I," came back at once from about half the recruits, and business had to be temporarily suspended.

A man residing on the outskirts of London was recently proudly exhibiting a new type- writer to his f,ther-in-law, who was up from the country on a visit. Ha tapped the keys for a minute ore' so to ,show his proficiency. "There! what do you think of that?" he asked. "Well," was the rural one's reply, " it's a fie instrument, and maybe it's 'igh-class music; but, bless yer, for somethin' touchin' you should 'ear my boy Jim on 'is melodeon."

A motor-car came pelting down the High. street of a little country town the other day, and in turning a c9rner at the bottom it collided with and knocked down a pedestrian who was carrying a basket of potatoes on his shoulder. Fortunately the fellow escaped with a few bruises, and when he had recovered somewhat a spectator said to him :—" That was a lucky get off, my man." " Yes, so 'twas," replied the victim, groping for his potatoes. " S pose I'd bin earryin' eggs?" •

DEAR CHILDREN, I am very glad to know that you appre- ciate the offer I made to send you a bottle of Mason's Extract, and quite a large number of Members have sent applications, and will by this time have received this little gift. I expect most of you are now enjoying your- selves to the full, either at the Seaside or in the lovely country, among the flowers and trees and birds. I hope you will have a very happy time. Be sure and write and tell me about all ithe things which interest you. Whenever I stand and watch a group of merry children at their play, I wonder whether any of them be- long to the Children's Corner League, and whether they would be delighted if I went up to them and said I was Uncle Ned. Some day, perhaps, I may be able to meet you all—then we shall have a delightful time • together. Such a lot of letters, so here goes. Alice Pilling wishes to join our League, and sends a splendid piece of advice, entitled, "Do it now," which I have printed below. Nellie Roberts wishes to thank me for .her Prize. I think she must know I am fond of kittens, for she forwards a very pretty post card with three dear little kittens, just saying "Good Morning." I should much like to have a post card from all of you this month, and I will award two boxes of Fry's Chocolates to the senders of those I consider the prettiest of all.
Now good-bye again for another week, Ever your affectionate, UNCLE NED.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l can scarcely tell you what a great surprise and-pleasure it was to me to find I had gained the first prize in the Pin- cushion Competition. I must thank you very much for the very pretty present you have awarded me. I like the brooch very much in deed, and every time I wear it I shall think of Uncle Ned. Again thanking you for your kind flees,
I am, sour loving Niece, OLIVE KINGDON.
DO IT NOW.
If you hake hard work to do,

Do ii now. . . If you have a song to sing, sing it now. Let the notes of gladness rine', Clear as song of birds in spring. 'Let every clay sonic music bring, Sing it now. If you have kind words to say, Say them now.
To-morrow may not come your way, Do a kindness while you may; Loved ones will not always stay, Say them now. If you have a smile to show,
'Show it now. Make hearts happy, roses grow, Let the friends around you know, The love you have, before they 'go, Show it now.

Whatever he decides upon, As sure as sticks are sticks, He will /not rest until he starts, We is only six. He thought he'd be a-doctor, So to prepare for that, I found him .making up bread pills,

A boot and shoe repairer next, Was what his lordship choose, And then I found the soles of my Best bocits were full of screws. • A painter was the next best thing Whtch came into his head; Our parlour carpet, which was green, He quickly changed to red. KOLAB'S BRAVEILY. Minnie was a little Eng Huh girl, who lived with her uncle And aunt, Mr. and Mrs. Cuth- bert, in India.

One day, Minnie and her „aunt Went out fol a walk, but tney had not gon.e far, when they saw a small crowd of natives, who were watch ing a large, strong Indian woman cruelly ill treating a little girl. Minnie's auntie, who knew the language,

asked her why she was whipping the child like that, whereupon the woman answered. ,"he has broken the water-pot, and must therefore be punished." Mrs. Culhbert 'ordered her to stop, and the Woman, fearing to disobey her, gave the child a sounding blow across the head, which knocked her down, and fled into, her hut. Mrs. Cuthbert then asked the little girl, who was crying bitterly, what her name was. "My name is Kolab," ansivered the child, looking with awe at Minnie .and her auntie. "I will tell you what," exclaimed Minnie, "Kolab, you shall come with me, and be my little ser- vant; I shall take care of you, maytet If Kolab's only answer was to burst into tears, and, kneeling down, Ithe elapsed Minnie's feet with, her hands, andigissed them fervently. . .

Not long after that. was Minnie's twelfth birth- day, and, as a present, her uncle gave her a little white pony, named Stella. The next day Minnie went for a ride on it; but, while passing under some trees, a mischievous monkey dropped a cokernut on Stella's 'head, whic,h frightened the pony so much., that it bolted.

Minnie held on Bice grim death; her face was very pale, and her hair was streaming behind in the wind. All the natives seemed thunderstruck, and never attempted to stop the frightened animal; but Kolab, brave little Kolab, iaw the danger. and, rushing up, caught the bridle rein, and eventually stopped the pony, but not until her poor little body was bruised and battered by being dragged along the road. Willing hands soon lifted Minnie out of the saddle, and willing hands soon carried Kolab home, and laid her on Minnie's little white bed. Presently, the doctor arrived, and said if she regained consciousness, she would live. Once she said, "Missy Babba," and then fell into a deep sleep, from which she awoke quite refreshed. The last thing that was heard of Minnie and Kolab was that' they were going to England in a week's time. —From LUCY' FITZPAIRICZ.

div.head: GENTLEMEN I
div.p: GENTLEMEN I

• General Lee !was in the car going to Rich- mond, and had a seat at the extreme end. The other seats were filled with officers and soldiel.s. An old woman of humble appearance entered at one of the stations, and finding no seat, and none having been offered her, approached the General. He immediately rose and gave her his seat. Instantly there was a general rising and proffering of seats to "Mass. Robert," but he calmly said.. "No, gentlemen; if there is no seat for the infirm old woman, there can be none for me." The effect was remarkable. One after another'got out of the car, as if the seats were too hot to eit on; and the General and the old lady' soon had the car before them to choose their seats. NELLIE BARNES.

ANNIE ROWLANID.

div.head: MY MOTHER.
div.p: MY MOTHER.

There's no one like my mother; She's all the world to me, Her love is like no other, So gentle, kind, and free. Her ftice is bright as summer, Her brown and watchful eyes, And music of her gentle voice, Makes home a paradise.

There's no one like my Mother; When far from home I stray, When dangers gather o'er me, And cares beset my way; The thought of her can cheer me, And put my grief to flight, Can...turn all sadness into joy find make the darkness light.

There's no one like my Mother; When pain has laid me low, None smoothed like her my pillow, Or soothed my burning brow; She watcheti so fondly o'er me, With never weary care; And won me back to health and joy With constant love and prayer.

There's no one like my Mother; When gladness fills my heart, In all my hopes, in all my joys, She bears the brightest part. • My star of childhood ever; The sunshine of my way, she'll be my guiding angel To Heaven's love•comPacl clay.

The World's Largest Touring Club, The Touring Club de France recently organized a fate to celebrate the extension of its membership to 100,00 p. The development of the great French club, which for years has been open to motorists and every other class of travellers, furnishes an object lesson in the possibilities of a progressive policy. Originally founded, like the League of American Wheelmen—a once powerful but now moribund body—in imitation of the Cyclists' Touring Club, the T.C.F. has extended its aims in every direction and has exerted an. enormous influence for good in many matters of importance to travellers in France. Had our own touring club followed a similar tendency, its scope and usefulness might have been greatly extended.

Little attention has been bestowed of late years upon the vagaries of the cyclist by the police, who have had their hands full trapping bigger game in the persons of motorists. But it behoves cyclists not to be lulled into false security, for a haul of cyclists, some thirty-one riders, were fined for furious cycling a few weeks ago at the North London Police Court. Some of the victims were ladies, who explained with surprise that they were not riding at 20 miles an hour. But the magis- trate pointed out to them that there was no question of a speed limit for cycling, and that under certain circumstances five miles an hour might be considered dangerous. It usually happens that trie police take action against cyclists only when moved thereto by local complaints respecting inconsid.mta riding/ The Superiority of the Cycle over the motor-cycle and the small car was forcibly brought home to me last week when I formed one of a party of five on a combined motor-cychw and photographing tour. One small car, one motor- cycle, and one push bicycle were used, and the journey covered about 600 miles. The car wanted repairs or attention about once in every 50 miles, the motor-cycle once in 150 miles, but the only repairs wanted by the push bicycle in the 600 miles had to do with one burst tyre, which took ten minutes to mend. On one occasion the car went wrong about five miles outside Bristol at 10.80 in the evening, and after vainly trying to discover the cause of the trouble in the dark, we had to finish a long day's ride pushing the car into town in the small hours of the morning.

div.head: Gears for Long-Distance Riding.
div.p: Gears for Long-Distance Riding.

Most experienced.distance riders adopt compara• tively moderate gears, and being good peclallers, are able to "get their feet round" with Celerity when the conditions are favourable to a higher gear than that employed. For example, to cite the cases of three notable tricycle road record breakers—Dr. Wesley uses 61 cranks and 68 gear, Drake si and 70, and Dudley Dayruond 61 and 64. Of course, on a safety with similar cranks, the gear wouldirange higher; but 70 to 75 gear, with 6-1 or Thecranks are found to yield excellent results in a distance ride over average roads. Most hills can be ascended without undue effort, and even a light opposing breeze does not make the work laborious. It is true that a few riders find themselves suited with long cranks and gears of 80 or 90; but the average cyclist regards the light, easy pedalling on a moderate gear as far, more pleasurable than the dull, sustained, if slower, slogging necessary with the higher ones, at one time favoured by wculd-be speedmen.

div.head: Prize Non,fikidding Tyres
div.p: A Prize Non,fikidding Tyres

It appears that the non-skidding tyre which won the prize of 000, awarded in the Cyclists' Touring Club competition, held early last year, has now been patented. There is little prospect, however, of any useful result proceeding from the club's outlay. Nearly all the devices purporting to abolish side-slip hitherto have been of a character repugnant to practical riders. Although side-slip remains an evil only to be avoided by skill and prudence in negotiating greasy roads, the risk is preferable to any attachment which spoils the efficiency of a pneumatic, thus adding to the labour and detracting from the pleasure of cycling. On ordinary surfaces the smaller tyres in use to-day are less liable to slip than were the larger ones of years gone by. This is due to the necessity of pumping them hardee than was the came with larger tyres.

A more simple process is to wash the peat, without destroying its natural fibrous state: and to mix the resulting moist mass with a mixture of hydrated lime and an aluminium compound, (as, for instance, aluminium sulphate) and press it in moulds for a short time in the moist state, after which the resulting plates are allowed to harden in the air. The resultant product needs only a comparatively low pressure, and this for only" a short time; and is then set out to dry in the air. The resulting artificial wood is not hygroscopic, and in order to use it for open-air work needs no painting or further impregna- tion. In view of the fact that the pressing operation takes only a few minutes, consider- able quantities can be manufactured in com- paratively small space and time.

LORD KELVIN'S CONCEPTION OF AN ATOM. Lord Kelvin, in an article on "Atom with Enormous Energy for Radio-Activity," published in the Philadelphia Magazine, puts forward a plan of an atom capable of storing an electrion (or negative electron) with enormous energy for radio-activity. The 'atom of ponderable matter is supposed to be intrinsically charged in concentric spherical shells, each such layer being uniform in itself, but the density and sign of the distribution varying from layer to layer. A curve, called the work curve, is then plotted, whose ordinates shew the work required to bring an electrion from infinity to the point in question. In the curve drawn there are two minima, one just within the radius of the atom and a second at its centre. Between these two minima there is one maximum. The curve is of course symmetrical about the centre of the atom. If, therefore, an electrion be placed at or near the centre of the atom, i.e., between the two maxima of the work curve, it has stability, but only through a nar- row range. If it is taken further away from the centre than these maxima, the electric force of the atom upon it will shoot it out of the atom with prodigious velocity, which will be but slightly diminished by the attraction of the whole atom when it gets outside.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
A • NEW INSULATOR.

Corticite, the new Portuguese heat-insulating material, has granulated cork for its principal oomponent, and it is claimed to be a perfect in- sulator, resisting the greatest extremes of climate and the attacks of insects, even of white ants. It caln be sawed and bored like wood. It is not inflarhmable, and is of value for many pur- poses. A covering of it for steam-pipes and boilers is claimed to effect a great saving of heat, correskondingly reducing 'the temperature of the boiler-room.

div.head: COMPRESSED AIR LOCOMOTIVES.
div.p: COMPRESSED AIR LOCOMOTIVES.

A novel use of compressed air is made by some railway companies in the Southern States of America. When the loads of cotton for export are being taken to the coast there is always some danger of such highly inflammable material becoming damaged through sparks from the locomotives. To prevent this, the locomotive boilers are filled with compressed air. A train load of several thousand bales of cotton can be hauled by these locomotives at a rate of twelve miles an hour, although no fire whatever is used in working them.

div.head: SELF-IGNITING MANTLE.
div.p: SELF-IGNITING MANTLE.

Platinum sponge becomes incandescent on con- tact with gas and causes its ignition. This pheno- menon has given rise to various arrangements for producing the flame direct. MM. Rouxeville and Michaud have patented in France a process in which the addition of any foreign apparatus to the mantle is avoided. They have recourse simply to a mixture in which platinum sponge is the essential ingredient, composed of refractory and adhering substances. Impregnated with this mixture in its upper texture, the mantle has the power of igniting the gas, and of thus becoming incandescent. The stem may also be covered with the composition, and the same result &soured.

EARTH-HEAT AND AIR RADIO-ACTIVITY. That the radio-activity of air may be due to the escape of emanations from subterranean regions, to heat' in the earth's interior causing the expulsion of negative ions from certain oxides, or to ions received from the sun, is sug- gested by /H. Nagaoka, in a paper on radio- activity and .geophysical phenomena, published in the Tokio Physico-Mathematical Society's Proceedings. The examination of tho smoke from the volcanoes is proposed as a source of in- formation which will enable us to decide the question. The possibility of terrestrial magne- tism being due to the rotation of the earth, the outer crust of which is electrified by the presence of ions escaping from the interior, is pointed out. Supposing that electro-magnetie mass could be detected by a balance, it follows that those atoms whose electrons are moving the most rapidly will be the heavier, and the ratio of the atomic weights will not be the ratio of the number of electrons. Deviations from Prout's law could thus be expected.
EYEGLASSES TO CURE COLOUR BLINDNESS. \ '

While glasses cannot fit the colour-blind for observing signals at sea or on railways, Herr Pichon, of Cologne, finds that much assistance may be given in distinguishing between colours. Persons, he says, having the common form of colour-blindness require red and green glasses, as the red glass absorbs green rays and causes red objects to appear lighter than to the naked eye, and the green glass absorbs red rays and adds to the brightness of green objects. Those who are colour-blind to yellow and blue can be similarly helped by glasses of yellow or blue. In cases of colour-blindness to all colours, three different glasses—red, green, and viclet—are necessary, and these can be combined in pairs so as to give twelve different shades, making possible very ac- curate determinations. In a special kind of colour-blindness, disease of the retina causes utter inability, to distinguish blue, and an affec- tion of the optic nerve makes it impossible to see red.

ARTIFICIAL WOOD FROM PEAT. Frequent attempts have been made to use peat as raw material for the manufactureof arti- ficial wood. The material must, for this pur- pose, be fully reduced to a fibrous condition, so as to produce a fibrous and a mealy mass.
