div.head: SEA SERPENTS.
div.p: SEA SERPENTS.

Is there such a thing as the "Sea Serpent"? The answer, says a Globe writer, depends upon what is actually meant by the question. If it means, Is there one gigantic species of marine- snake answerable for all the recorded appear- ances of the so-called sea serpent? the answer must be in the negative. If, on the other hand, the question means, Is there a marine creature hitherto unknown to science which might give rise to such reoords? the answer is that there are probably many sea serpents. For there is little doubt that a number of huge creatures hitherto unknown to science live in the depths of the ocean, and some of them may be serpents. The sea serpent, however, May be more nearly related to the extinct Mosasaurus, the sea ser- pent of the Cretaceous times. Mosasaurus had a long, snake-like body, with the fore and hind limbs in the form of fin-like paddles. It some- times attained a length of 75ft. According to Dr. A. Gunther, the mosasauriane "form the nearest approach in Nature to the modern creature of the imagination, the 'sea-snake.'" And it is pos- sible that the mosasaurus of Cretaceous times may have left descendants in the present ocean. It is to be remembered, however, that while the sea serpent is problematical, an "airy nothing," which may eventually obtain a "local habitation" in our museums, and a name in the records of science, there are really many well- known "sea snakes." They form the family Hydrophidte, that is, water snakes, and number some fifty species. They are found in the tropical parts of the Indo-Pacific Ocean, chiefly in the neighbourhood of the Persian Gulf, in the East Indian Archipelago, and between China and Northern Australia. They are the most poisonous Of all bilaaes, iruquelitii.g Lne neignuournoon ox land, but never leaving the water, with the ex- zeption of the genus Platurus. Never exceeding 12ft. in length, these sea snakes can never be taken for that huge monster, the sea serpent.

LETTERS TO THE EDITOR operations are being watched very keenly by Mr . Haldane, the Secretary of State for war. The general idea is that under cover of darkness an invading force makes a raid upon the south coast,having NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. ; the knowledge that the regular defending army is partly beyond the-seas and partly on the east coast. Authors of letters intended for publication must in The raiders, under command of Colonel Kent, V.D., all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor will consist of the Hampshire Volunteer Infantry as a guarantee of good faith. Brigade (6,000). with guns,and the cyclists of the Home Counties Brigade (700). They will land at Swanage and try to do as much damage as possible before the defenders can concentrate. These will consist of the cyclists of the five Infantry Volunteer Brigades now encamped on Salisbury Plain (the Gloucester and Somerset, Worcester and Warwick, West Yorkshire, Staffordshire. and the 30th Field Army Brigade), 1200 in all, and also the 400 cyclists belonging to the Ist and 4th London and the 24th Field Army Brigades encamped at Beaulieu. In addition to these the infantry of the Home Counties Brigade now at Lulworth are to help in the destruction of the invader. The main object is to ascertain under conditions as realistic as peace permits the value of cyclists in obtaining and transmitting intelligence.

div.head: HOLIDAY TRAGEDIES. CHILD FALLS FROM A BLACKPOOL
div.p: HOLIDAY TRAGEDIES. CHILD FALLS FROM A BLACKPOOL
TRAIN.
Mother's Fatal Heroism.

The August Bank Holiday was marked by one of the most terrible fatalities which has ever occurred in this district. Shortly after four o'clock on Sunday afternoon an excursion which was proceeding from the Potteries to Blackpool by the London and North Western Railway, was passing Weaver Junction, between Acton Bridge and Preston Brook, It was. travelling very rapidly when the communica- tion cord was pulled and the train was immediately brought to a standstill. Several officials and passengers rushed down the line and found two passengers —Elizabeth Bradbury (32), of 65, Well- street, Hanley and her five-year-old son, Harold Reginald —lying there shockingly injured. Mrs. Bradbury had both her legs cut off above the knee while the little boy's right foot was severed. How the accident happened is a mystery. It appears that Mrs. Bradbury, her husband, Abraham Bradbury, who is a potter's placer, and the child were travelling in a first-class carriage along with Mr. and Mrs. Albert Scott, also of Hanley, and their three children. All intended spending a week at Blackpool. Mr. Brad- bury was looking out of the windoyv when he heard a scream, and on turning round saw the carriage door was open and his wife and child missing. No-one actually witnessed the accident, but it is conjectured that the child was playing with the door handle and suddenly managed to turn it, the door opening and throwing him out on the line. The mother, frantic with grief, dashed after him. When the train had been stopped a telegraph message was sent to War- rington and medical aid was procured. The mother and child were afterwards with all haste taken on to Warrington in another train and Call- veyed to the Infirmary in the police horse ambulance. It was at once seen that Mrs. Bradbury's condition was hopeless and she passed away at eight o'clock. The child is progressing as favourably as can be expected. The terrible affair created a great sensation and the deepest sympathy is felt with the husband in his sudden loss. The news of Mrs. Bradbury's death was imparted to her aged mother as soon as it was received, and Mrs. Keay was prostrated by the shock- ing intelligence. Another sad feature is that for some time past a young Irish lady, a cousin of Mrs. Brad- bury, had been on a visit to the family in Well-street. Her holiday expired on Monday morning, and she was just about to the return journey to Ireland when the telegram announcing her cousin's death was received. Overwhelmed with grief, she was quite unable to take the strain of the long journey, which she has consequently been compelled to abandon.
THE INQUEST.
A juryman said it would take 15 or 16 lbs pressure to turn the handle.

Sergeant Barlow (coroner's officer) said he could turn I ' it with two fingers in the ordinary way. A child of five could turn it easily. John Hebden, mechanic, said be had examined the handle and it was in perfect order. William Bennett, foreman at Warrington station, said he axamined the handle a minute or two after the arrival of the train at Warrington, and there was nothing defective about it. The Coroner, in summing up, said the accident was very lamentable and they all deeply sympathised with Mr. Bradbury. The only question for the jury was whether anyone was to blame, and they had to bring their business knowledge and their knowledge of the world to bear. They had travelled, as he had done, in a carriage containing twice as many people as there ought to be in. It was absolutely impossible to keep children under control in a railway carriage for they were always wanting to be at the door and to look through the windows. They wanted to be examining things, and he was very glad that they did. It was curiosity that enabled them to imbibe knowledge and make themselves men of the world. The jury would remember the old-fashioned days, when in order to get out of a train they had to drop the window, get hold of a dirty carriage handle and turn it. All that had been obviated by placing handles inside and it was a very great convenience to the travelling public. They could not blame the com- pany for having inside handles because if they did away with them the public would be the first to complain. No doubt there was some danger attached to them, but they could not have anything in this world without some degree of dangar. In this case, too, everybody knew of the danger. The jury deliberated in private and on their return the foreman said they had agreed that the affair was a pure accident and did not attach any blame whatever to the company. Mr. Bland expressed the sincere regret of the company at the accident and said they had heeu anxious to throw whatever light they could on the sad affair. They hoped the child would recover. The Coroner said that travelling as he did on the company's system and seeing what took place, he was surprised at the percentage of fatalities on the line. It was not the wonder that people were killed but that they were not killed. He was surprised the company managed to carry such a great number of people with- out more fatalities taking place. The travelling public did not look after themselves but the company's officials looked after them very well indeed. Mr. Bland : It is very kind of you to say that and I am sure it will be very gratifying to the company. The jury also expressed their very sincere sympathy erith the father in his trouble.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, August 11, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, August 11, 1906.
CYCLISTS SHOCKING DEATH AT LONGFORD

A distressing fatality occurred at Longford on Mon- day when Charles Hill (56), colliery engine tenter, 19, Park-road, Golborne, methis death whilst cycling when close to the Longford Hotel. It appears that on Sunday evening the deceased and his son-in-law, Albert Unsworth, 21, Park-road, Golborne, arranged to go for a cycle ride the following dey to Frodsham. They set out 'about 7.30 on Monday morning and reached Longford about half an hour later. Here they had to pass two wagonettes and Unsworth took the lead. A number of boys were running alongside the vehicles and one of them collided with the back wheel of Hill's machine with the result that he was knocked off and fell under- neath the leading wagonette, the back wheel of which passed over his head, death being almost instantaneous. At the inquest, which was conducted by Mr. S. Brig- house at the Longford Hotel, on Wednesday, Mr. Unsworth stated that about 30 years ago the deceased lost his left arm as the result of au accident. Mr. Hill was fond of cycling and was a capable rider. When passing the second wagonette witness took the lead. He rang his bell to warn the lads who were running alongside the vehicle but the boys would not move. He succeeded in getting past when he heard the deceased shout " Heigh up," and next heard someone scream. He looked round and saw the deceased lying in the road- way with his head covered with blood. Witness went to Warrington for assistance, and the police ambulance was sent. Deceased did not move after he fell. No blame could be attached to the driver of the wagonette and the fault rested solely with the lads " who were fooling about." Edwin Jones, Ashton-road, Golborne, who was on the wagonette at the time of the accident said one of the lads ran into Mr. Hill's machine with the result that he was thrown off. He fell between the wheels of the vehicle ' and the back wheel passed over his head. Had the ,I deceased not lost his left arm he would have been able I to save himself. Mr. Brighouse : These lads are a perfect nuisance. I Witness : They are and they want stopping. Henry Craven a lad of about ten years of age said another lad bumped into him and knocked him on to Mr. Hill's machine. Mr. Brighouse: This is a very sad calamity but we must not blame the lad's too much. Boys will be boys and perhaps we did the same when we were boys. Neither can any blame be attached to the driver, and had it not been for the deceased's physical infirmity he would have heen able to save himself. A verdict or" Accidental death" was returned. Mr. Brighouse expressed sympathy with the relatives of the deceased.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

The championship of the West Lancashire League will soon be decided, and Warrington will indeed be fortunate if the honour rests with them. Earlestown are fully determined to capture the cup, and their pros- pects are exceedingly bright. By their easy victory over Stanley on Saturday they placed themselves at the head of the League,Warringtou being just one point be- hind. Both teams have still a match to play, so that the position is full of interest. If Warrington are to become champions they will have to vanquish Prescot while Earlestown will have to be beaten in their encounter with St. Helens ROM The odds therefore are greatly in Earlestown 's favour, for if both teams are victorious, Earlestown will still have a point to spare and will secure the championship. The deciding matches take place away on the ISth inst.

Warrington had to submit to a particularly severe drubbing at the hands of Bowdon on Satitrday. This is the second time this season that the Bowdon eleven have been their conquerors and Saturday's defeat was quite staggering. The Warringtonians were unfortunate 11 in being able to place only a weak team in the field whereas the Cestrians were very powerfully represented. Going to the wicket first, Bowdon piled on 201 for the loss of only 5 wickets and then declared. The Warring- ton response was poor, the whole side being dismissed for 104.

On the Warrington side T. Wright maintained the capital form which he has shown this season. He hit out vigorously and had made 3) before he was run out. The bowling of J. Pattison gave the Warringtonians a great deal of trouble, that player accounting for five wickets at a cost of 26 runs.

Warrington 2nd visited Bowdon and the match ended in a draw. Batting first, th 6 visitors applied the closure at 173 for the loss of G wickets, the Warrington captain (E. Pierpoint) being the top scorer with 38. His brothers R. and R. G. Pierpoint each batted in fine style for their innings of 30 an P. Taylor gave a faultless display for his 26 (not out). Bowdon lost five wickets for 06 runs,their most successful batsman being C. E. Dalton (29). E. Pierpoint bowled effectively, taking three wickets for 15 runs.
Penketh tried conclusions with Arley Park and triumphed by a majority of 34. The scoring was not high, the best efforts being those of Ward (15) and Hodgkinson (13).
Bervsey-road Wesleyans find defeated Fairfield, the feature of their innings being Jolley's 31.

It is not often that cricket elevens tie, but that was the result of the match between Rylands Bros b and the " Gnardian " °Mee who each made 43. On Monday the Warrington Thursday met the " Guardian" team, the game ending in a draw.

Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Ltd., trounced the Haydock Lodge eleven in unmistakable fashion. The Lodge batsmen were all dismissed for the miserable total of 19, the bowling of W. Norman and J. Dargon being practically unplayable. Norman captured seven wickets for four runs, and Dargon three for 12. The Brewery men ran up 133 with 9 wickets doiAn and declared. J. Milner (32 not out), T. Allen (23 not out), H. Cook (20) and J. Dargon (13) batted in first-rate style -- There will be a great attraction at Arpley this (Saturday) afternoon in the shape of the final of the Works Competition. The contesting teams are Pearson and Knowles and Walker's Brewery and as both have acquitted themselves remarkably well throughout the competition a very keen struggle is anticipated. Wickets will be pitched at three o'clock and each side will play fifty minutes.

Bowling. After an excellent fight the Cemetery Hotel Club have been put out of the running for the Lancashire and Cheshire County Championship. In the inter- mediate rounds they carried everything before them, and up to a late stage on Saturday it looked as though they were going to defeat Leigh Railway in the semi- final. With seven men off the green they held the lead, though only by a small margin. T. Bolton and H. Harrison were then associated, and the result of the Fame was as surprising as it was unexpected. Bolton is one of Warrington's most capable trundlers, but he was unaccountably off colour and going down 21-4. Leigh Railway claimed a big advantage. The remaining Cemetery men strove hard to wipe off the arrears, but the task was beyond them, and though they all won their games Leigh claimed the match by a margin of two points,

On account of the holidays, play in connection with the Works Competition was last week-end suspended. The programme will be resumed this (Saturday) after- noon when further progress will be made in the fourth round, and also in the consolation competition.

Cycling. Ideal weather favoured the holiday week-end and cyclists had some delightful outings. Seven members of the Warrington Club took part in a tour through the far-famed WyE and Severn valleys and visited such interesting places as Shrewsbury, Hereford, Ross, Gloucester, Twekesbury, Tintern, Chepstowe and Mon- mouth. The scenery in these parts is really charming and all were agreed that a more enjoyable holiday could not have been arranged. Another party visited some of the most beautiful parts of North Wales, calling at Rhyl. Conway, Bangor, Carnarvon, and back by the Pass of Llanberis, Bettws-y-coed,Llangollen, Bannor-on-Dee, and Whitchurch. Everyone came back delighted with I the outing and expressing the opinion that ere long I another similar tour would be undertaken.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL.
Business of To-Night's Meeting.

Owing to the August Bank Holiday the meeting of the Warrington Town Council which in the ordinary course would have been held on Tuesdly evening, was postponed until this (Friday) evening at six o'clock. The business for consideration includes the following :
WATCFI COMMITTEE.
Councillor Sankey is recommended for appointment as a member of this committee in place of the late Alderman Roberts.
FINANCE AND ESTATE.
• LEASE OF LAND -LOAN FOR STREET WORKS.

At a meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee an application having been made for a lease of the laud behind the Education offices,the site of stables recently demolished, was considered, resolved that the land be let to the Warrington Motor Carriage Co., Limited, on a lease for flve years; and afterwards subject to three months notice, at a rental of £2O ss. per annum, the lessees to undertake not to carry on any business on the land which would he an annoyance to the occupiers of the Education Offices.
The Town Clerk laid before the meeting the sanction of the Local Government Board to the borrowing of sum of £1,501 for works of Private Street Improve- ment.

At a subsequent meeting a farther letter was read from the Warrington Motor Carriage Co., Limited, and after discussion it was resolved, that they be offered the whole of the land between the Education offices and the boundary wall for a five years tenancy at .£2.G per annum, and they also be charged ss. per annum acknow- ledgement for the right of way up Garven-place. The Company have since notified their acceptance of these terms.
THE Tux MR. A. EDELSTEN'S ACTION AGAINST THE CORPORATION.

The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee on July sth discussed at considerable length the agreement with Colonel Edelsten, and it was ultimately decided that the opinion of Counsel should be taken as to the position of the Corporation: The case first being sub- I'mitted to the Committee.

At a meeting on 19th July, the case for the opinion of Counsel respecting the action commenced by Mr. J. A. Edelsten against the Corporation and Mr. William Bolton was submitted to the Committee :—Resolved that the Mayor be empowered to obtain independent professional advice and assistance with regard to his position in the action. Mr. Segar Owen and Mr. F. R. Pierpoint attended with regard to the strip of land required for the widen- ing of the south side of Friars'-gate. After hearing their views the Committee decided to offer the sum of £7 for the land, and to allow Mr. Pierpoint to build up to the prescribed line, and in the alternative Mr. Pier- point must set back to the line of frontage of the adjoin- ing premises. Resolved, that the new road leading from Wilderspool to the bridge over the Runcorn and Latchford Canal be called Loucher's-lane. _ _
Resolved, that Chapel-street on the north side of Queen's Gardens be re-named Palmyra-square.
BROOK POLLUTION.

The Medical Officer of Health submitted a report that he had received from Air. Ruddock with reference to the pollution of Orford Brook.—ResoTved, that the Sanitary Inspectors be instructed to take samples of the stream in order to ascertain the source of the nuisance.
That the Medical Officer of Health was instructed to withdraw the notification of chicken-pox.

Melbourne, Limited for the supply of a concentrator shaft at Long- ford Depot at £42 be accepted. A SEWERAGE DIFFICULTY. Mr. ildermanEvans attended the Paving and Sewer- age Committee with reference to the capacity of the Fennel-street sewer and the nuisance consequent upon its being unable to cope with the sewage of the district. It was resolved,that the Borough Surveyor be requested to report as to the best means of relieving the sewers on the east side of the town emptying into the river at Bank Quay. Resolved that the Local Government Board be re- quested to grant their sanction to the paving of that portion of Sankey-street opposite the late Miss Garven's premises. The Town Clerk reported that he had now received the sanction of the Local Government Board to the borrowing of £1,501 for the making up of certain streets which had been withheld owing to non-settlement ()- objections.

Resolved that the Committee cannot entertain the same. The tenders of Mr. Thomas Stringer for the forming and paving of Parr-street at £713 2s. 7d. and the foot- path in Navigation-street at £29 lßs. At a meeting of the Museum Committee it was resolved that an extra Student's Ticket be issued to such borrowers from the Lending Library as desire it,l to be available (under the usual rules) for any books ; except works of fiction. It was reported that the number of books iSsued from the Lending Department during the year ending 30th ' June was 87,256, an increase of 10 per cent. on the previous year. TOWN HALL, PARKS AND DATIIS COMMITEE. THE QUESTION OF SWIMMING INSTRUCTION. At a- meeting of this committee the report of the Bathkeeper WELS read, from which it appeared that the income from the Baths for the past six weeks was £lO2 lls. 7d., end for the corresponding period last year £139 4s. 7d., decrease £36 13s. The;receipts from the Bowl- ing Green for the past six weeks were £2l Ss. 2d. Councillor Wilkinson having resigned his membership of this committee resolved, that Councillor Craik be appointed in his place. A deputation from the Education Committee, consist- ing of Councillors Evans, Pemberton, and Wilkinson, attended and discussed with the committee the question of teaching swimming to the children from the public elementary schools of the Borough. Resolved that the Bathkeeper be instructed to report fully on the matter. Permission was given to the Soldiers' Memorial Com- mittee to construct the foundations in Queen's Gardens for the War Memorial. THE DESTRUCTION OF THE WEIGHING MACHINE. TRADESMEN AND MARKET ACCOMMODATION. The Markets Committee met for the purpose of con- sidering the question of a new weighing machine at Bridge Foot, the old one having been destroyed by an accident. Resolved that a new machine capable of weighing 20 tons be provided and that the London and North Western Railway Co. be approached by the Town Clerk with regard to a proposed site adjoining the premises on the south of Arpley-road. A deputat:on from the Warrington Tradesmen's Association,consistiog of Mr. William Roberts and Mr.J. Pendlebury, attended the committee with reference to the proposed extension of the market. They con- tended that he present market accommodation was ample for the requirements of the Borough, and that before the Committee decided upon a definite scheme of extension they would like to know the objects thereof. _ .

The Deputation having withdrawn, after discussion,it was decided that they be informed that this Committee do not contemplate any further extension of the market at present, and they were informed accordingly. At a subsevent meeting a letter was rdad from MO, T. The Borough Surveyor, in accordance with a resolu- tion of the Committee, produced a plan showing the stalls as at present set out in the market. div.head: FIRE AT WHITECROSS_ WORKS.
div.p: THE FIRE AT WHITECROSS_ WORKS.

The Fire Engine Commiteee considered the question of the fire at Whitecross Works, certain rumours having reached them as to the delay of the Brigade in reaching the fire, and in order to give publicity to the matter it was resolved that the following report of the Superin- tendent be published :—" I beg to report that at 1.20 p.m. on Saturday last the " Hooter " at the works of Messrs. Crosneld and Sons, Limited, was sounded, and being Saturday, the majority of the members of our brigate assembled at the station in case their services were required. I immediately telephoned to that firm asking if they had a fire, the man in charge replying that the fire was at Whitecross. About twenty minutes later a cyclist from the National Telephone Office arrived at the station to inquire if our wire was out of order, as the Whitecross Co., Limited, had been ringing us, and we had not respondßd to the " Call." I informed him that the bell ou the telephone at the Fire Station had not rung, which can be verified by the firemen who were at the Station. We then went into the office, whilst Engineer Wakefield rang up the " Central." He was informed by the operator there that the Whitecross Company had called ten minutes ago. I then telephoned to the Whitecross Company and asked if they had rung us up, and was informed they had done so. We were told their (the Whitecross Co.'s) intention was to ask us to COMO and "stand by" as the brigade from Nlessrs. Crosfield and Sons was already on the scene, and on our informing them that our brigade had been waiting in readiness, they thanked us for doing so. I then again rang up the " Central " twice, and found the wire in working order. At 1.55 p.m. a cyclist arrived from Whitecross and said that Mr. Bacon, the foreman en,iner9 had sent for our assistance. We at once turned out with the steamer " Captain," but on arrival found that the Patent House, where the fire had occurred, was burnt down, and our services were not required. At a later stage I made inquiries at the Telephone Office, when the Manager promised to have the matter looked into, as the operator at that time was not on duty, but up to the present I have received no report. I have since had an interview with Mr. Walter Milner, of the Whitecross Company, with the object of elucidating the affair, when he stated that no telephonic message had been sent to us from his firm. The Committee were of opinion that no blame attached to the Brigade.

div.head: Wesley Guild Ramble.
div.p: Wesley Guild Ramble.

On Monday a successful ramble in connection with the Bewsey-road Wesley Guild took place, fifty or sixty members and friends visiting Whitley. A very pleasing feature of an enjoyable afternoon was that the Guild was admitted to the gardens of Mr. Fletcher which are now at the height of perfection. The visitors were most kindly received and entertained by Mr. and Mrs. Fletcher and the outing was thoroughly appreciated.

div.head: ACCIDENTS ON THE CHESHIRE LINES.
div.p: ACCIDENTS ON THE CHESHIRE LINES.
Warrington Ilan Killed at Trafford Park.

Two serious,abcidents occurred on the Cheshire Lines Railway on Thursday. In the afternoon John Riley, of 4, Naylor-street, Warrington,a drainer in the employ of the Company was working at Trafford Park when he was caught by the Liverpool express and killed instantaniously. Shortly before midnight, Driver Richardson was shunting near Battersby-lane railway bridge when he noticed a fellow employee,James Whalley (34),Lydiate, Southport, lying near the medals. The man's feet had been badly crushed and he was at once taken to the Central Station, first-aid being rendered by Porter Robertson. The man was then taken to the Infirmary where it was found necessary to amputate one of his feet. Deis progressing favourably.

Big .Ship Canal Developments. Important developments at the Manchester end of Ship Canal were indicated at the meeting of the Canal Company in Manchester on Thursday. The running of two well-known lines of steamers to the port has enabled a commencement to be made with the impor- tation of frozen produce, and a sorting chamber is to be constructed to give facilities for the requisite quickness of cargo discharge. The deepening of the canal from 20 to 28 feet is progressing, and between Eastham and Partington will be accomplished in about three weeks.) It was further mentioned by Mr. Bythell, the chairman, that a flour and provender mill was to he opened in Trafford Park next month, and another is to be established. Cotton imports to Man- chester this season show a decrease of 210,000 bales, but as Liverpool has a decrease of nearly 800,000 bales the reduction (caused by the smaller crop) has not been abnormal. Mr. Bythell advised spinners to form amongst themselves a large importing agency, with a stock in Manchester.

div.head: Beautiful Warrington.
div.p: Beautiful Warrington.

Sir,—One of the chief hindrances so far experienced by the Beautiful Warrington Society in the carrying out of its mission has been the want of some place where the various materials necessary for town garden- ing can be procured. Everybody who has the slightest experience of gardening knows how hard it is to find where such things as soil and manure can be obtained, or to transport them where they are wanted. To meet this difficulty we have at length suceeeded in establish- ing a depot at Factory Yard and secured the services of a man whose duty it will be to arrange for the collection of any material which may be offered suitable for the purpose of the society including not only soils, mould, turf—lime we have already in quantity—manure, bark and boxes but trees, shrubs, plants, cuttings, roots,bulbs and seeds. If anyone, therefore, has such things which he is willing to place at the society's disposal for distribution among its members all that will be necessary is to send a post-card to the Superintendent Beautiful Warrington Society's Depot, Factory Yard. and be will make all arrangements for collection.—' a.m, Yours etc.
K. E. MARKEL.
August 70,190 G.

div.head: Nurses.—An Appreciation.
div.p: The Nurses.—An Appreciation.

Sir,—Warrington to-day is the proud and enviable I possessor of two noble institutions, notably, the Infirmary and the Nursing Association. The efficiency of the institutions depends upon the excellence of their respective committees and working staffs, and the untiring energy displayed by them. As is well known each institution is particularly fortunate in being in the happy possession of an admirable working staff, without which it would be utterly futile to endeavour to cope with the work which is constantly increasing. It was with great surprise and no little regret that I learned the other day,that the Nursing Association were, about to lose three of the most valuable of their work-' lag staff. The three to whom I refer, are Miss Whit- field (the respected matron) who came to Warrington at the time of the inauguration of the nursing movement nine years ago when the only means of locomotion there was by trudging on foot. It meant, downright hard wearing work such as only one who entered whole- heartedly in the work could have done. The scene of her labours, lay in St. Austin's Ward (Livernool-road and Sankey Bridges,) where she by her kindly forbear- ance and tact speedily won her way into the hearts of the people, amongst whom it was her lot to minister. Since her appointment as matron she has by her sterling qualities, rendered unto the Borough those services which she has been eminently qualified to give. Nurse Jacocks has also given nine years' service to the Borough. Her scene of operations has lain principally in Latchford Ward, among the people of which district there is not to-day a more valued and highly respected person. Nurse Leshaw, by her eight years' ministering service amongst the people of St. John's Ward, has given entire satisfaction and wherever her work has lain, she has met with the greatest possible esteem and respect. So much has she ingratiated herself into the hearts of the people amongst whom she has laboured, that keen regret is felt on :all hands by her coming severance from the people of her Ward. I have known of cases where patients (who by the way have been tended with loving care by the nurses) and their friends, have often wished to present to the nurses some lasting present, though small it may be, just to show in their homely way, their kind appreciation to them for the valuable work that they have done for them, but to the honour and credit of the whole of the nurses be it said, that not in any singleinstance has it been known of any such present being accepted by them, but as is usually the case it has been pointed out to them that if they wish to give at all,they might give to the Home, in however small a degree and their gifts would be willingly received and acknowledged. Thus the nurses have at one and the Caine time done a double work for the Borough. They have gone about their work (which has been well and carefully done) in a happy kind of way and at the same time, where a timely hint has been needed, as above, it has been given. When one takes into consideration the length of service they have given and how they have toiled (often when they have been unwell themselves) through pouring rain, hail, frost and snow, one cannot help but feel that the thanks of the whole community are due to each of than for the best years of their lives that have been devoted to the cause of suffering humanity while they have been resident here in Warrington. Yours,&c.,

div.head: FREE CHURCHES AND THE EDUCATION QUESTION. --- Interview with the Rev. Thomas Law.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES AND THE EDUCATION QUESTION. --- Interview with the Rev. Thomas Law.

NO MORE CONCESSIONS. The National Free Church Council hag from the first been on active participant in the Education fight, and in order to ascertain the position of the Free ChurcheS now that the Education Bill has passed.its second read- ing in the House of Lords, a representative obtained LI interview with the Rev. Thomas Law the Secretary the National Council. Mr. Law has been snendiPgPsit of his holidays in Thanet, and, was passing, tbroug London on his way to the North of England. iv to an " The House of Lords "said Mr. Law, in VT"' 11 a enquiry as to how matters stood "has read the that second time without division but no one supposes al the question is decided. His my opinion that the battle will take place in the autumn, and that there Wl' have to be some hard fighting if a satisfactory measure is to be passed." " How do the Free Churches regard the Government measure ?" Mr. Law was asked. " We regard it as an honest attempt to settle a vexed. question in a just and equitable manner. Mr. ,Birrelt has deserved the thanks of the whole nation for the statesmanlike way in which he has pilotted the measure through the House of COMMOII9. At the same time it would he idle to deny the strong feeling of the Free Churches that the Government has gone as far as it possibly can go in the way of concessions. Clause 4, for instance, is viewed with grave dislike by our members. The National Free Church Council has been fully alert on the matter throughout the year. We have had to closely watch the development of the Bill, and have taken all possible action. No one can say what will happen in the autumn, but I cannot conceal my belief that there is trouble ahead. We shall be exceedingly active in the autumn. There every probability that the National Free Council will be specially summoned immediately the Education Bill comes back from the Lords, and the action of the Free Churches will be decided by representatives from every part of the country. It is perfectly certain that anY attempt to make serious concessions will mean that Nonconformity throughout the entire country would be solid against the Government's accepting them. I am perfectly sure that the alterations in the measure outlined by the Primate, the Duke of Devonshire and others during the debate in the House of Lords could not be accepted by us. We feel that the utmost limit of concessions has been reached, and thst there must be no further atte apt at compromise on vital principles:

After Sir Gilbert Greenall's recent successes in ,Pig-breeding there can be no doubt at all that he is a whole-hogger !" * * I wish to say to the congregation, said the minister, " that the pulpit is not responsible for the error of the printer on the tickets for the concert in the Sunday School room. The concert is for the benefit of the Arch Fund, not the Arch Fiend." * * * ik The gentleman who advertised this week for a wife tvith small means " with one leg preferred " leads us tO doubt his motives. Already a widower, he appar- ntly desires to become a widower for the second time. At any rate he is looking out for a wife with one foot in the grave. • * Good luck to Crosfield's Band which departs this Saturday night for Calais! The intention of these workingmen musicians is to cement the entente oordiale and give the Calais-donians a rare musical treat. Both cement and music of the right sort are eing taken in goodly quantities. Colonel Edelsten's writ against the Mayor and Town 'rk for the specific performance of the agreement to base the pin mill, and claiming damages, is intly going to end in a lawsuit. The Mayor is -0 empowered to obtain professional advice and assistance with regard to his position in the action. At any rate there will be "costs !" * * * If revolution on resistless wing Abolish law and order, Church, and King, One man would still maintain The ancient law, That fine old crusted Tory— Bernard Shaw. " Tatler." • * The garden allotments adjoining Longford Gas Works are being put to excellent use. Almost every inch of the land is under cultivation and quite a heavy crop of vegetables has been yielded. There are also one or two beds of flowers but their fragrance is somewhat lost in competition with the other odours for which the neighbourhood is famous. * * There is a record profit of ,V 14,000 on the working 1 the Gas Department for the year ended March 31st. and revenue have both gone up considerably. engineer suggests a sort of depreciation account meet extraordinary expenses incurred in renewal Plant." Nothing is said about reducing the price gas to the consumer, and we quite anticipate a oral outcry from this quarter. , It has always been one of our standing jokes in country to scoff at the bride's cooking. But in ,orway they have taken the joke seriously and a new Its' now provides that every bride must be certified as able to cook. This is good for the husbands, better still for the future generation, but bad for the doctors. Their only hope will ho in the enthusiastic bride cooking " not.wisely but too well." * • * - Two Committees of the Town Council, and one of ' the General Purposes Committee which corn- the whole of the Council, have had a lengthy sion on the question of a donation from the igh funds to the Infirmary, but no decision has arrived at. Whatever wisdom there may hemn a ttitude of councillors, there is obviously little use. vs the Council, as a Council, at its meeting this ty night,may carry matters somewhat further. * * In the engineering section of the British Association Wednesday Mr. Mackenzie dealt with waterproof is as a solution of the dust problem. He con- that there was only one solution of the problem was satisfactory and permanent, and that was t!) have a road made of proper dustless materials. It certainly becoming increasingly obvious that tPalliatives such as water and calcium chloride are no Jae. The remedy lies solely in up-to-date scientific methods of road construction. * * we are S . not surprised at the complaints of Cheshire wieh t In regard to the dust nuisance. On the North- cars o Chester main road on Bank Holiday the motor ti and thoir accompanying dust cloud were a posi- ve horror. There was a car every two or three Ininutes, and to cycle along the road was an excruciat- ing form of running the gauntlet. No wonder the owner of one estate is having a belt of trees and Shrubs planted round his fields to protect the corn and grazing. * * With the official opening of the Fishguarcl and ,Itesslare Railway and Harbours, another thoroughfare has been added to the existing highways between this F.onntry and the adjacent island.—" 'Cork Constitn- ional."—" This country and the adjacent island " !asparticularly good from an Irish point of view. One !Ziand is as good as another evidently. We suppose People of the Isle of Man will adopt similar l Nraseologv. They have more reason to do than our ri • - sh friends, seeing that they possess a Government 11,! their own, and may therefore claim to be a country."

One day a gentleman gave half a ere:mu to al! deaf and dumb" beggar, who, quite taken offi his guard by such unusual munificence, ex- claimed, joyously, "Bless you, sir! Bless you!"':- " Halloa!" said the old gentleman; " I thought was. " you were deaf and dumb?"" So I sir, replied the beggar, " but your extraordinary generosity was such a shock—such a pleasant shock—to the system that it has 'restored my speech and hearing. Bless you again, sir, a thousand times !" " I thought all the toasts to-night were to be of a light and amusing nature?" " They are." " But you have Binks down for a topic that is decidedly heavy and serious." "Of course'. If there is anything funnier than Binks trying to tackle a great principle that he doesn't fully understand, I don't know what it is." Teacher :"And why are you so late, Tommy?" Tommy: "If you please, teacher, it is mother's washing-day ; she lost the lid of the copper, so I have been .sitting on. the top to keep the steam in." " Now, boys," said the schoolmaster, " what is the axis of the earth?" Johnny raised his band promptly. " Well, Johnny, how would you describe it?," " The axis of the earth," said Johnny, proudljr, " is an imaginary line which passes from one pole to the other, and on which the earth revolves." " Very, good !" exclaimed the teacher. " Now, could you hang clothes on that line, Johnny?" "Yes, sir," was the reply. " Indeed !" said the teacher, disappointed'; " and what sort of clothes?" " Imaginary clothes, sir !" , They sat in the dress circle, eating chocolates between the acts of the matinee. "Mary says I paint," said the firet girl. "The horrid thing !," "Never mind what Mary Says," the other answered in a soothing voice. "If she had your complexion she'd, paint, too."
